editorials.title: Many layers: On onion produce, issues
editorials.passage:
Since the 1960s, India has developed a balancing-act habit: between keeping food prices affordably low for consumers and assuring farmers of remunerative prices, with the state’s interventions focused on managing this volatility in the short term. This is also why the government banned onion exports from December 2023 to May 2024, then imposed a $550/tonne minimum export price and a 40% export duty, reduced the duty to 20% in September 2024, and finally abolished it in April 2025 . But erratic weather together with the lack of long-term relief has rendered the act increasingly awkward. From farmers’ point of view, the government often changes its mind after they have made important production-related decisions based on the expected price. On the other hand, during the bounteous rabi harvest, onion farmers in Maharashtra, the country’s principal supplier, had argued that the Centre’s procurement price of ₹12.35/kg would not cover the costs of cultivation. The Centre subsequently raised the price to up to ₹26.45/kg, but many farmers — including some who had had to sell at ₹1/kg earlier because of low quality and lack of storage, among other factors — were unable to capture the higher value, exposing the limits of intervening after prices have already collapsed and not reaching all farmers or grades of produce.

While the government has alluded to some price manipulation, the dominant issue remains that it keeps reacting instead of taking proactive measures, including improving storage options, maintaining a less erratic trade policy, moving stock more efficiently between regions, and protecting farmers against price shocks. The abnormal rainfall at the time of harvest and a 5%-7% drop in the kharif crop in Maharashtra, together with the well-known challenges associated with storing onions and maintaining large buffers, are simply among the pressures that highlighted the flaw this year. Further, Tamil Nadu’s targeted subsidy, to buy 1,000 tonnes of onions to distribute 1 kg per ration card at ₹35 , will impose pressures on the Centre to maintain a steady supply. The move is commendably designed to discourage hoarding while allowing private retail prices to cool down. However, the State must also guard against the pitfalls of distributing onions through a dry-grain PDS network — its economic case could collapse if post-harvest losses, to which onion is more susceptible than, say, wheat or rice, exceed 10%-15% — and if the need arises to persist with the subsidy. Finally, if other States also adopt similar measures, the Central buffer could be quickly exhausted, more so given this year’s high storage losses of around 30%.

editorials.title: Orthodoxy redux: On Keralam, religion and Muslim women’s rights
editorials.passage:
Veteran Islamic cleric Kanthapuram A.P. Aboobacker Musliar ’s directive to restrict Muslim women’s participation in public celebrations has unsettled Keralam because it strikes at a fundamental question: women’s right to participate in public life. This is not merely a quarrel over how Muslims should mark Prophet Muhammad’s 1,501st birth anniversary. It is a test of how far religious authority can intrude into the lives of women in a State that takes pride in its progressive social history. Kanthapuram says he is merely reminding followers of established religious norms. His supporters argue Milad celebrations have moved beyond mosques and madrasas into large public events, and that scholars have a duty to caution against such departures. That argument holds no weight. Communities have the right to preserve traditions and regulate religious practices, but they have to conform to the values enshrined in the Constitution. When women are told to remain at home because their presence could cause “chaos”, the issue is no longer about religious observance; it is at variance with constitutional equality and Keralam’s long struggle to expand the space in public life for women disadvantaged by social customs and religious traditions.

The Muslim community is not a monolith. It contains both orthodox and progressive currents. More Muslim women are breaking barriers in education, employment, politics and public life, but that progress is encountering a counter-current of renewed orthodoxy and social control. The CPI(M), Keralam’s main Opposition party and a decades-old ally of the Kanthapuram-led faction of Samastha Kerala Jamiyyathul Ulama, a body of Sunni scholars, has responded sharply. The Congress, which leads the ruling coalition, was largely guarded until Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan rubbished the decree as antediluvian. The Indian Union Muslim League’s silence is harder to defend. A party with an active women’s forum and a woman legislator for the first time in the State Assembly cannot equivocate when women’s right to public participation is open to challenge. Its caution may reflect political pressure over Waqf, Vande Mataram and PM-SHRI, or an attempt to improve ties with the Kanthapuram faction amid strained relations with the rival Samastha faction. Whatever the political calculation, silence carries a cost. Religious freedom does not confer on religious authorities the right to regulate women’s freedom of movement, association and degree of participation in society. During Onam, social media were awash with videos of young Muslim girls celebrating the harvest festival. Kanthapuram’s remarks drew criticism from a section of Muslim women on social media. Keralam cannot claim to be progressive while making exceptions for orthodoxy.

editorials.title: Beyond Bishkek: Strategic bid to shape region's architecture
editorials.passage: The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation is entering a consequential phase on its silver jubilee. The Bishkek Declaration reflects a bloc moving beyond its traditional security mandate towards connectivity, economic resilience, technology and wider Eurasian cooperation. For India, that evolution presents a clear opportunity, but also a test of whether New Delhi can move from participation to agenda-setting.The bloc’s condemnation of the US-Israeli strikes on Iran adds a sharper geopolitical edge to the declaration. By backing Tehran and invoking the UN Charter, the grouping has reiterated its push for a more multipolar world order. However, the declaration’s strongest signal is on terrorism. SCO members rejected “double standards” and approved regulations for a coordination body to fight regional terrorism. Prime Minister Narendra Modi called for dismantling the entire ecosystem of terrorist financing, recruitment, radicalisation and safe havens, warning against States that use terrorism as an “instrument of policy”—a pointed message to Pakistan..The larger opportunity lies in shaping the organisation’s emerging economic and technological agenda. The declaration highlights transport corridors, multimodal connectivity, digital commerce, energy security, industrial cooperation, startups, national-currency settlements and resilient supply chains. These are areas where India can press for tangible outcomes: interoperable digital systems, streamlined customs, logistics cooperation and greater access for Indian businesses to Eurasian markets. Technology is an equally important frontier. The SCO’s focus on artificial intelligence and information security gives India a chance to shape regional norms rather than simply adapt to them. The security dimension will be crucial, too, particularly on cross-border terror, narcotics and transnational crime. Yet, India should be realistic about the SCO’s limitations. Its members have sharply divergent strategic interests, making consensus for a communiqué easier than implementation. It should be judged more by what it delivers, not by the breadth of its declarations.For New Delhi, the most important shift is geographical. With Central Asia gaining greater prominence within the SCO, India should make the region the centrepiece of its engagement, combining political outreach with connectivity, education, healthcare, energy, technology and cultural partnerships. At 25, the SCO has gained considerable geopolitical weight. India should neither turn it into an arena for bloc politics nor allow others to unilaterally define its agenda. editorials.title: Karnataka Bill clarifies apartment owners' rights
editorials.passage: A Bill recently passed by the Karnataka Assembly has brought a degree of relief to flat owners who have had to deal with ambiguities in their rights and responsibilities in a shared property. The Karnataka Apartment (Ownership and Management) Bill, which rationalises two earlier statutes, has largely been welcomed by apartment owners and associations in the state’s fast-growing cities. It proposes to expand the law’s purview to integrated townships, high-rises, mixed-use complexes and gated communities. The clarity was a longstanding demand of dwellers who had little say in builders’ plans and were plagued by inconsistencies in rules. The Bill addresses issues such as ownership and use of common areas, calculation of maintenance fees, enforcement of bylaws and resolution of community disputes. It mandates the builder to hand over common areas and their management to an elected association. Community and commercial facilities would be reserved for the exclusive use of apartment owners and dwellers. Importantly, it considers future development following changes in floor area ratio and zonal regulations, and the use of terraces for which the rights earlier were presumed to remain with the developer. Alterations and redevelopment would now require the consent of at least three-fourths of owners in a housing complex. The Bill also requires promoters to disclose mortgages taken on the project land, which frees buyers from liabilities before the property is transferred..Until now, urban societies were governed by two 1972 Acts in managing apartments before and after construction. Builders took advantage of the previous laws’ loopholes to construct ‘builder floors’, illegal additions with dubious documentation, or commercialise the common area. The undivided land share remained unspecified, allowing the developer to put up more structures and reduce the owners’ rightful share of land. Now, the onus would be on the builder to ensure structural safety, obtain occupancy certificates, form an apartment owners’ association within three months, execute transfer deeds and hand over corpus funds and security deposits. Failure to comply could attract penalties.While a few land rights activists claim the Bill does not fully comply with the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 and should be challenged in court, apartment buyers can rest easier that the new law, coupled with RERA, would put them in a far safer legal ground..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: Quick Take | Women off welfare grid
editorials.passage: Ramabai Ranveer’s story reflects both the grit of India’s people and the glaring shortcomings of its governments. The 47-year-old widow and mother of two girls in Beed, one of Maharashtra’s poorest districts, recently ran 3 km to win ₹3,000, which she plans to use on her daughters’ textbooks. While Ramabai’s barefoot run earned admiration online, it also painted a grim picture of Indian women struggling to make ends meet despite so many welfare schemes aimed at them. Like most other states, Maharashtra has a number of programmes to support women from modest backgrounds, including Majhi Ladki Bahin and Kanya Bhagyashree. But as the cases of Ramabai and thousands of women recently rendered ineligible for state assistance in West Bengal show, the gap between a scheme’s announcement and implementation is filled with immense pain..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: Mining revenue must be the means, not end
editorials.passage:
There is a basic economic truth that India cannot afford to ignore as it races towards becoming a developed economy: when the cost of an essential industrial input rises, the burden rarely stops at the source. A higher tax on coal can mean higher power costs. A higher cost of iron ore can translate into more expensive steel. Higher steel and cement prices raise the cost of roads, bridges, railways, housing, automobiles and virtually every major infrastructure project. 

This is why the Mines and Minerals Amendment Act, 2026 must be understood not as a narrow dispute between the Union and the States, but as an important intervention in India's national economic architecture. At its core, the legislation addresses a simple question: can essential mineral inputs be subjected to an increasingly fragmented patchwork of State-level taxes and cesses, with the eventual cost being borne by the entire Indian economy? For a country investing in infrastructure and manufacturing on an unprecedented scale, the answer has to be no. 

The immediate context for the legislation is the landmark nine-judge Constitution Bench judgment of the Supreme Court in July 2024 in Mineral Area Development Authority v. Steel Authority of India. By an 8:1 majority, the Court held that royalty is not a tax and affirmed the power of States to tax mineral rights under the constitutional scheme. The judgment was constitutionally significant. But it also created a new fiscal possibility: mineral-producing States could seek to impose additional taxes and cesses on mineral rights and mineral-bearing land, over and above existing royalty and other statutory payments. 

Jharkhand was among the States that moved rapidly to exploit this newly clarified fiscal space. Parliament has now sought to establish a more predictable national framework. This distinction is crucial. The amendment is not about taking away States’ legitimate mining revenues. The Union government has maintained that States continue to receive the overwhelming share of mining-related revenues. The issue is the proliferation of additional levies that can raise the effective cost of extracting and using minerals. Consider the economic chain. 

Iron ore may be extracted in Jharkhand or Odisha, but the steel manufactured from it is used across India. Coal mined in Jharkhand does not merely serve Jharkhand; it feeds India's electricity and industrial ecosystem. Limestone mined in one State ultimately b ecomes cement used to build infrastructure in another. Minerals are therefore not ordinary local commodities. They are foundational national inputs. India is building highways, freight corridors, ports, airports, railways, power plants, homes and defence infrastructure at extraordinary speed. 

The national economic interest therefore requires mineral prices and industrial input costs to remain competitive and predictable. If every mineral-producing State begins adding its own taxes and cesses, the country risks creating a race in which each jurisdiction seeks to extract more revenue from the same national supply chain. The cost does not disappear. It moves forward - from the mine to the manufacturer, from the manufacturer to the infrastructure developer and ultimately from the economy to the consumer. A mineral tax imposed locally can therefore create an economic cost nationally. The MMDR amendment recognises this fundamental reality. 

The politics surrounding the legislation are particularly revealing in Jharkhand. Following the Supreme Court judgment, the Hemant Soren government enacted the Jharkhand Mineral Bearing Land Cess Act, 2024. The resulting revenues became substantial. According to figures cited by the State government, collections were around Rs 1,379 crore in 2024-25 and rose sharply in 2025-26. Soren subsequently argued that mining-related revenues constitute an exceptionally large component of Jharkhand's own revenues and warned that the new legislation could deprive the State of thousands of crores. There is a legitimate argument here about fiscal federalism. 

Mineral-rich States must receive a fair return from the resources extracted from their territory. But another question deserves equal attention: What should a government do when it receives a sudden, extraordinary stream of revenue from a finite natural resource? The economically prudent answer is clear: a substantial part should be converted into permanent productive assets. Mineral wealth is finite. Roads, irrigation, power infrastructure, schools, hospitals, logistics networks and human capital are investments that can outlive the minerals that financed them. 

This is where Jharkhand's record warrants scrutiny. The State has substantially expanded recurring expenditure, including large welfare commitments. Its 2025-26 Budget, for instance, allocated Rs 13,363 crore to the Maiya Samman Yojana and around Rs 5,000 crore for free electricity, while revenue expenditure substantially exceeded capital expenditure. The point is not to argue that welfare spending is illegitimate. A government must protect vulnerable citizens. The larger issue is fiscal composition. A government sitting on an extraordinary natural-resource revenue stream should use it to accelerate capital formation and raise the State's productive capacity. 

It should build the infrastructure, skills and industrial ecosystem that allow future generations to prosper even after the mineral deposits decline. The available fiscal data do not establish that every rupee of additional mining revenue was squandered. But they do raise a legitimate question about whether Jharkhand has converted its exceptional mineral opportunity into an equally exceptional investment push. That question cannot simply be dismissed as partisan politics. There is an unmistakable irony in the present controversy. The Soren government used the fiscal space created by the 2024 Supreme Court judgment to impose a new mineralbearing land cess. 

Parliament has now exercised its constitutional authority to establish greater uniformity in the mineral-tax regime. Yet the same Chief Minister has launched a political campaign portraying the legislation as an assault on Jharkhand’s rights. Soren has announced a statewide agitation, while JMM has warned of escalating its protest. One can understand a Chief Minister defending the fiscal interests of his State. But there is a larger question that needs to be asked: Is a mineral buried beneath Jharkhand's soil economically relevant only to Jharkhand, or does it form part of India's national industrial ecosystem? The answer is obvious. 

Jharkhand's coal powers industries far beyond its borders. Its iron ore feeds steel production that supports infrastructure throughout India. Its minerals enter national supply chains. Federalism cannot mean that each State is free to impose an unlimited fiscal burden on inputs that are indispensable to the national economy. Equally, national economic integration cannot mean depriving mineralproducing States of legitimate revenues. The obje ctive of the MMDR amendment is to strike precisely this balance. The most unproductive way to view this legislation is through the familiar prism of Delhi versus the States. India needs strong States and a strong Union. 

It needs cooperative federalism, not competitive fiscal extraction. States must receive substantial and predictable revenues from mineral development . Mining-affe c te d communities must b enef it . Environmental costs must be properly accounted for. But Indian industry must also have a stable and competitive mineral regime. That is what a mature federation should seek. There is an even larger lesson here. India cannot become a developed economy simply by extracting more minerals. It must convert mineral wealth into human capital, physical capital and productive capacity. The true measure of a mineral-rich State is therefore not how much additional tax it can impose on a mine. 

It is how much additional prosperity it can create from that mine. Coal should become reliable energy. Iron ore should feed globally competitive steel. Mineral revenues should finance infrastructure, education, healthcare and industrialisation. Resource wealth should become a foundation for prosperity rather than an excuse for ever-expanding recurring expenditure. 

This is ultimately the significance of the Mines and Minerals Amendment Act, 2026. It seeks to ensure that India's mineral wealth does not become trapped in a fragmented regime of competing fiscal claims, raising costs across the national economy. For India to become a developed nation by 2047, its minerals must serve not merely the State in which they are found, but the national economic transformation that they can make possible. That is not an assault on federalism. It is an assertion of the economic logic of a functioning federation. 

(The writer is a national spokesperson of BJP and an acclaimed author)

editorials.title: Alignment, not alliance
editorials.passage:
Viewing the maritime security agreement that India and Japan recently inked in New Delhi through the lens of China simplifies its understanding. The two countries share motivations stemming from a more aggressive China, their economic dependence on open sea routes, and a mutual desire to prevent any one nation from controlling the Indo-Pacific region. Viewing the new agreement solely as an anti-China coalition ignores its actual significance. 

India and Japan are forming a significant strategic alignment, mirroring alliances seen in the evolving international order, though without a formal treaty. In this respect, the operational nature of the arrangement between Rajnath Singh and Shinjiro Koizumi, the defence ministers, is what gives it import. The concept of a free and open Indo-Pacific has been discussed for years, but concrete actions are now backing it. Under the terms of the framework, the Indian Navy and the Japan Maritime Self-Defence Force will work together more closely on everything from search and rescue and disaster relief to humanitarian assistance and the sharing of information and maritime-domain awareness. 

The agreement provides for naval visits and exercises, personnel and expert exchanges, and the use of port and repair facilities, as well as logistical support. Taken in isolation, these are hardly revolutionary measures. Taken together, they amount to something of strategic consequence: the start of an interoperable maritime relationship. The difference is a meaningful one. One thinks of alliances in terms of formal pacts and the like, not least the undertaking to come to each other’s military aid if attacked. In the present-day Indo-Pacific, strategic alignment has a different dynamic. States will exchange information and make themselves logistically compatible; they will exercise and learn to operate in concert, but there is no treaty obligation to go to war. 

This is where the India-Japan partnership is heading. Geography is the reason for it. India holds a commanding spot in the Indian Ocean, and Japan is located close to the eastern limits of China’s maritime periphery. The Malacca Strait and the Indian Ocean lie between them, with some of the most vital sea lanes in the world for the transport of manufactured goods, commodities, and energy. Freedom of navigation is thus a matter of national and economic security, not an abstraction. 

China is part of the equation. With the People’s Liberation Army Navy extending itself into the Indian Ocean and Beijing’s activities in the East and South China Seas, the strategic picture for Delhi and Tokyo has changed. However, the impact is not the same. For Japan, the western Pacific and the East China Sea are of immediate concern. India has the added continental problem of its Himalayan border dispute with China and a maritime worry over the Chinese build-up in the Indian Ocean. Cooperation is all the more compelling for such differences. Identical threat perceptions are not called for, only overlapping interests. Safeguarding sea lines of communication is a case in point. 

With improved awareness, a deeper understanding of the extensive maritime domain is possible. More advanced exercises will allow the armed forces of both countries to know one another. They can develop capabilities in logistics, unmanned systems and mine counter-measures that will be valuable in a crisis, and yet neither has to cede any strategic autonomy. We also need to look at the industrial side. Discussions are occurring about merging Japanese technology with India’s expanding defence manufacturing capabilities, such as in shipbuilding. 

With Japan’s defence transfer rules under review, new possibilities are emerging that were unimaginable a decade ago. This makes the UNICORN integrated communications antenna system for ships noteworthy, even beyond the project's scale. This marks a political milestone, as it is the first transfer of this nature between them. India and Japan have a history of strong diplomatic and economic relations, but their defence-industrial collaboration has been more cautious. A stronger material basis for the relationship will be established if momentum is generated in partnerships concerning shipbuilding, production, research and development, or technology transfer. 

It is worth examining the agreement more closely. Both countries show an interest in developing networks beyond just bilateral relations. The trilateral naval exercise with Indonesia at the beginning of the year is one example. Again, the collaborative efforts in Indo-Pacific logistics and humanitarian assistance demonstrate a more comprehensive perspective on regional security. Through initiatives like the Quad, exercises such as Dharma Guardian and JIMEX, and defence cooperation with the United States and Australia, these collaborations are constructing a layered security system for the Indo-Pacific. 

One would be hard-pressed to compare this with the alliance system of the Cold War era. There is no centralized command, no headquarters, nothing in the way of an automatic collective-defence commitment. Instead of a hierarchy, it is a networked order where states collaborate in different configurations for distinct goals, like one group focusing on maritime surveillance and another on supply chains and technology. India finds this approach to its liking. New Delhi has taken pains to show that strategic autonomy is not forfeited by deepening relations with Washington, Canberra or Tokyo. 

Its continued dealings with Russia and membership of the BRICS and Shanghai Cooperation Organization are testament to a reluctance to be cajoled into any inflexible bloc. In the India-Japan dynamic, strategic distance is not a prerequisite for autonomy. A nation may have no formal alliance but still work with partners of choice on defence technology, intelligence, or logistics, exercising political discretion in how it uses those capabilities. In a multipolar world, the essence of autonomy is the option to partner rather than to shun it. Japan is also changing. 

Tokyo’s security perspective has expanded beyond its post-war strategic culture. Driven by worries over China's military power and exposed sea lanes, Japan has become willing to play an active part in regional security. The willingness to transfer defence technology and equipment indicates a change. There is no indication that a military pact between the two countries is close. Nor is it right to cast every cooperative venture as a means of containing China; doing so would be to miss the public goods that come from maritime cooperation, from search and rescue and disaster relief to making shipping safer and protecting commercial routes for smaller states in the Indo-Pacific. 

However, to suggest China has no bearing on the matter would be unrealistic. Geopolitics does not have a vacuum in which to create its institutions. Sometimes the best way to balance is without the pretence of a balancing coalition. What makes the new accord between India and Japan noteworthy is that it defies either extreme: it is not simply a memorandum exchanged by friendly governments, nor the germ of an Asian NATO. 

More subtly, it is the steady building up of operational familiarity, access and information between two powers in the Indo-Pacific whose interests are converging. That is how balancing is done in the new order, through networks where states can be intense in their cooperation and yet leave themselves room to manoeuvre, as opposed to fixed blocs arrayed against one another. 
 

(The writer teaches at Jadavpur University, Kolkata, and was the Eugenio Lopez Visiting Chair at the Department of International Studies and Political Science at Virginia Military Institute, US)

editorials.title: When a part of us dies silently
editorials.passage:
Language is far more than a collection of words and grammatical rules. It is the living memory of a people, carrying their history, beliefs, customs, songs, stories, and unique understanding of the world. Every language reflects a distinct way of thinking and interpreting reality. Yet, in our rapidly globalizing world, thousands of these linguistic treasures are disappearing, often silently. 

The last speakers of many endangered languages are living witnesses to cultures that may vanish forever when they are gone. Linguists estimate that nearly half of the world's approximately 7,000 languages are endangered. Some are spoken by only a handful of elderly people, while others have fewer than a hundred fluent speakers. Every few weeks, somewhere in the world, a language falls silent forever. Unlike the extinction of an animal species, which often attracts global attention, the death of a language usually goes unnoticed. Yet its loss is equally irreversible. Languages disappear for many reasons. 

Economic opportunities often require people to adopt dominant languages such as English, Mandarin, Spanish, Arabic, or Hindi. Parents may encourage their children to speak these languages, believing they offer a better future. Migration to cities, globalization, intermarriage, and the influence of television, cinema, and the internet further weaken the use of local tongues. In some cases, governments have historically discouraged or even prohibited indigenous languages in schools and public institutions, leaving generations disconnected from their linguistic heritage. 

The disappearance of a language is not merely the loss of vocabulary. It is the loss of an entire worldview. Indigenous languages often contain detailed knowledge of medicinal plants, farming techniques, weather patterns, and local ecosystems accumulated over centuries. Many possess words and expressions that have no equivalent in other languages because they describe experiences unique to a particular culture. Oral traditions, myths, folk songs, and rituals are deeply rooted in language. 

Once a language dies, much of this cultural wealth becomes inaccessible. The story of the last speakers is often deeply moving. Imagine an elderly woman who is the only person left capable of speaking the language she learned from her parents. She remembers lullabies, proverbs, and stories that no one else understands. She carries within her a library that has never been written down. When she passes away, an irreplaceable chapter of human civilization disappears with her. 

Such stories are unfolding across continents - from the indigenous communities of the Americas and Australia to remote villages in Asia and Africa. India, celebrated for its linguistic diversity, also faces this challenge. The country is home to hundreds of languages and dialects, many of which are spoken by small tribal communities. Several are now endangered because younger generations increasingly shift to regional or national languages for education and employment. The loss of these languages would diminish India's remarkable cultural mosaic. Despite these challenges, there is hope. Modern technology has become a powerful ally in language preservation. 

Audio and video recordings, digital dictionaries, online archives, and mobile applications allow endangered languages to be documented and taught. Universities and linguistic organizations work alongside native communities to record grammar, vocabulary, folklore, and oral history. Some communities have established language nests, where children learn directly from elder speakers, helping to revive traditions that seemed destined to disappear. However, preservation cannot rely solely on scholars or governments. Communities themselves play the most vital role. 

A language survives only when it is spoken at home, sung in festivals, used in daily conversations, and passed naturally from one generation to the next. Pride in one's mother tongue is the strongest safeguard against extinction. Protecting endangered languages is not an exercise in nostalgia. It is an investment in humanity's intellectual and cultural diversity. Just as biodiversity strengthens ecosystems, linguistic diversity enriches human civilization by offering multiple ways of understanding life and solving problems. Each language is a unique voice in the great conversation of humanity. 

The last speakers of endangered languages remind us that every language matters, regardless of how many people speak it. Their voices are not echoes from a fading past but urgent calls to preserve the richness of human expression. If we allow these voices to disappear, we lose not only words but also wisdom, identity, and history. Saving endangered languages is, ultimately, an act of preserving the collective heritage of humankind. The writer is a Thrissur-based accountant and freelance contributor

editorials.title: Sovereignty Vote
editorials.passage:
Iceland's rejection of renewed negotiations on joining the European Union is a reminder that, even in an age of mounting geopolitical anxiety, national sovereignty remains a more potent political force than the promise of collective security. The referendum came at a moment when the arguments for closer European integration might have appeared unusually compelling. 

Russia’s growing activity in the Arctic, uncertainty over the durability of American security commitments and the strategic tensions surrounding Greenland have all made the North Atlantic a region of renewed geopolitical importance. Iceland, a NATO member without a standing military, has obvious reasons to seek stronger institutional anchors. Yet Icelanders chose otherwise. By a narrow but decisive margin, they rejected even the reopening of negotiations ~ a preliminary step rather than membership itself. The reasons reveal something important about the limits of geopolitical logic. For Iceland, the European question was ultimately not about abstract ideas of continental solidarity or military cooperation. It came down to control. 

Fishing, which remains central to the country’s economy and national identity, became the symbol of a larger anxiety: whether decisions fundamental to Iceland's future would remain in Icelandic hands. That sentiment cannot simply be dismissed as provincialism. Small nations often understand sovereignty differently from large ones. For countries with centuries of secure statehood and substantial geopolitical weight, pooling sovereignty in supranational institutions can appear a rational bargain. 

For a small island nation whose modern identity was forged through a struggle for independence, sovereignty is not merely a constitutional arrangement. It is part of the national story. The referendum also exposes a recurring weakness in the politics of integration. Supporters tend to make technocratic arguments: larger markets, lower costs, monetary stability, institutional access and enhanced security. Opponents, meanwhile, ask a simpler and more emotionally powerful question: who will be in control? The latter question is harder to answer with statistics. 

This does not mean Iceland has turned its back on Europe. It already participates in the European single market through the European Economic Area and belongs to the Schengen zone. Its choice is therefore more nuanced than outright isolationism. Iceland appears to prefer cooperation without surrendering the maximum possible degree of political autonomy. That distinction may hold lessons for the European Union. The assumption that a more dangerous world will inevitably drive countries towards deeper integration is questionable. External insecurity can just as easily sharpen concerns about national control. 

When the world becomes unpredictable, electorates may seek the reassurance of institutions closer to home rather than more distant centres of authority. Iceland’s vote is thus bigger than a dispute over fish or EU membership. It demonstrates that global uncertainty does not automatically weaken nationalism. Sometimes, it strengthens it. For Brussels, the message is uncomfortable but clear: integration cannot be marketed merely as a rational response to danger. Unless political leaders can persuade citizens that shared sovereignty enhances rather than diminishes national control, even the strongest strategic arguments may founder on a simple democratic instinct ~ the desire to remain master of one’s own destiny

editorials.title: Balloon War
editorials.passage:
War has a way of making obsolete technologies new again. In Ukraine, one of the world’s most technologically intensive conflicts is now finding uses for an invention that predates the internal-combustion engine: the balloon. Reports that Ukrainian forces are using balloons to carry FPV drones towards Russian positions point to something larger than an ingenious battlefield improvisation. 

They illustrate how the economics of modern warfare are changing. The decisive question is increasingly not who possesses the most sophisticated weapon, but who can combine available technologies most imaginatively. The reported technique is deceptively simple. A balloon carries a drone across part of the distance, conserving its battery. Once near the intended area, the drone can be released and directed towards a target. 

Reports from Russian military sources suggest such systems have been used against logistics routes in occupied southern Ukraine, extending the reach of relatively inexpensive FPV drones beyond their operational range. There is a brutal economic logic to this. Modern air-defence systems are enormously expensive. Radars, interceptor missiles and combat aircraft are designed to defeat sophisticated threats. But an adversary can impose costs simply by sending large numbers of cheap objects into contested airspace. A balloon need not be invulnerable to be useful. 

It may be enough that identifying, tracking and destroying it costs the defender disproportionately more than launching it cost the attacker. Ukraine has become particularly adept at exploiting this asymmetry. Unable to match Russia aircraft-for-aircraft or missile-for-missile, it has turned necessity into a doctrine of innovation. Maritime drones have challenged the Black Sea Fleet. Long-range drones have struck oil refineries and industrial infrastructure far inside Russia. 

Operation Spiderweb demonstrated the vulnerability of strategic aircraft to comparatively cheap unmanned systems positioned close to their targets. The balloon is part of the same intellectual tradition: do not compete symmetrically when asymmetry offers a cheaper route to the same strategic effect. This does not mean balloons are a revolutionary weapon. They depend on weather, wind and favourable conditions. 

They lack the reliability and precision of missiles. Nor should every claim emerging from a battlefield saturated with propaganda be accepted uncritically. Yet their importance lies elsewhere. Military establishments have traditionally equated technological superiority with expensive and complex platforms. The Ukraine war is challenging that assumption. Artificial intelligence, commercial communications technology, cheap drones and even nineteenth-century aeronautics can be combined into systems that impose serious problems on a conventionally superior adversary. 

The future battlefield may therefore look less like the science-fiction visions of defence contractors and more like a technological bazaar: sophisticated software attached to cheap hardware, civilian devices adapted for military purposes, and old technologies given new life by modern networks. That should concern every military planner. Superiority may no longer belong simply to the side with the best weapons. Increasingly, it may belong to the side clever enough to discover that an old weapon, used differently, is not old at all.

editorials.title: Unholy nexus
editorials.passage:
Two days after a minister of the West Bengal government caused a media furore by castigating a pavement dweller for boiling milk for her children on a public thoroughfare, a leading Bengali daily published a telling photograph on its front page. The photograph was quite clearly not a candid shot but carefully staged to convey a political message. It showed a lady on her haunches cooking on a kerosene stove on a public footpath, and beside her sat a small boy engrossed in a book.

The message was unambiguous: there is a life for those who live on the streets of Calcutta, and that life isn’t bereft of dignity.

The tale of the pavement dweller ticked off by a minister did not end with media coverage. Sensing a possible backlash centred on possible charges of class insensitivity, the chief minister stepped in and promptly offered to relocate her to a more settled dwelling. The gesture was meaningful. Apart from emphatically asserting that his government — and, by extension, the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party — wasn’t lacking in compassion, the underlying message was that eviction from public spaces must be accompanied by rehabilitation.

This principle has been extended to the handling of hawkers who have taken over pavements adjoining all major roads of the city, much to the chagrin of shopkeepers who have found their trade seriously diminished. Indeed, it would not be inaccurate to suggest that the near-total disappearance of clear pavements is substantially responsible for a large section of the middle classes shifting their custom to either shopping malls or, more likely, online.

In many cities, the serious truncation of the right of pedestrians would have triggered a sharp response from organised taxpayers. In the case of Calcutta and its adjoining urban sprawl, attempts to free public spaces from encroachments have encountered political resistance. The attempts by the BJP government in West Bengal to remove hawkers from the major roads were met with resistance from the Left and remnants of the old Trinamool Congress regime. The hawkers were also supported by powerful sections of the media that have never quite adjusted to the new realities of post-May 4 West Bengal.

Over the past five decades, as Calcutta’s importance as an economic centre fell steeply, the political forces linked to earlier dispensations heralded the exponential growth of this new informal sector. Anecdotal evidence indicates that a section of city councillors controlled the deployment of street dwellers and hawkers and even set the terms of the underground rental market. Since the 1970s, the systematic violation of all the rules that governed the life of metropolitan cities became the new normal in Calcutta.

Another feature of this derailment was the capture of Calcutta’s public parks by private players. Whereas the earlier rationale of public parks was as breathing and recreational spaces for residents, places for kids to play, and venues for sports clubs, this was quickly modified. In the past decade, neighbourhoods have complained of residents being denied access to large sections of parks which have been contracted to private academies and institutions with an insatiable appetite for grabbing extra space, not to speak of replacing grassy greens with steel and concrete. Those familiar with Deshapriya Park and Vivekananda Park in South Calcutta will know the details of this grotesque disfigurement. The Rabindra Sarovar Stadium, once the pride of South Calcutta, witnessed sporting facilities being allowed to go to seed and rooms being given to clubs whose only claim to relevance was their proximity to TMC leaders.

An associated feature of Calcutta’s steady transition to dysfunctional anarchy was the rise of a real estate mafia with political connections. Once it was established that municipal regulations and, indeed, all norms were transactional, the city experienced the rise of a breed of ‘promoters’ who were ready to supplement their business interests with strong-arm tactics. In the last five years of the TMC government, the convergence of unethical real estate business and the ruling party touched Himalayan heights. As a newly elected MLA from a constituency that incorporates many prime residential locations, I have my hands full dealing with complaints from people (usually senior citizens) who have been harassed, intimidated, short-changed and outrightly cheated by either real estate sharks or political dadas . The problem has become truly acute as localities have been depopulated and are now over-dependent on senior citizens. Some of their tales of harassment are truly heart-rending.

The sanctity of contracts, the respect for property rights, and faith in the law and law-enforcement bodies — all essential features of a modern, vibrant economy — have been seriously compromised. This, in turn, has fuelled the perception that West Bengal is a ‘difficult’ place to do business. This image played a big role in the inexorable marginalisation of the state from the rest of India.

Like a well-groomed individual who abruptly stops caring, Calcutta systematically lost its civic pride. Yes, there was a deep love for the warmth and the culture of the former second city of the Empire — a reason why Rajiv Gandhi’s “dying city” remark triggered a wave of genuine outrage. However, this fierce attachment did not prevent a steady exodus of young people from the city to places that offered better opportunities and livelihood. Unfortunately, the cadence of those who voted with their feet was often drowned out by the shrillness of the claque that benefited from both depravity and decline. Those who organised (for a consideration, of course) the encroachment of business enterprises on public spaces managed the settlement of hawkers in pathways that belong to pedestrians and facilitated the capture of properties for ‘developers’ with cosy relationships with councillors will be loath to see a state and a city being run on the strength of rules. They will conceal their endorsement of rotten practices through an expedient advocacy of povertarianism and the romance of deprivation.

West Bengal’s road out of decline, dodginess and despondency faces many obstacles, some of which will necessitate a display of political will and far-sightedness. However, nothing is more important than a radical break from a culture that celebrates shoddiness and unending compromises with excellence. When Calcutta was dubbed the City of Joy, the suggestion was that human relationships can endure amid squalor. That overriding sense of compassion is indispensable. Yet, the indomitable spirit of the city doesn’t imply that decrepitude should become the defining hallmark of modernity.

Swapan Dasgupta is the finance minister of West Bengal. The views expressed in this article are personal

editorials.title: The ice bomb is ticking
editorials.passage:
Imagine a clear, sun-drenched afternoon in a high mountain valley. The sky is a piercing, flawless blue. No storm brews on the horizon. There is no warning rumble of thunder. There is no sudden downpour. Down below, kids are walking home from school. Farmers are working in their terraced fields. Then, out of nowhere, a roaring wall of water, mud, and heavy boulders bursts around the bend. It stands several storeys high and destroys everything in its path in seconds.

This is not a scene from a Hollywood movie. For families living near the peaks, a glacial lake outburst flood or GLOF is a sudden, terrifying reality. Mountain experts have a simpler name for it: an invisible tsunami.

The true terror of a GLOF is its complete detachment from local weather. A catastrophic wave can smash through a river valley thousands of feet below on a perfectly sunny day. It can blindside downstream communities. This happens because the actual trigger took place hours earlier and miles away. On August 16, 2024, the historic Sherpa trekking village of Thame in Nepal’s Everest region became a casualty of this mountain gamble. A massive rock avalanche slammed into the upper watershed miles above. The villagers could not see or hear it. The impact set off a violent chain reaction and broke two natural ice dams. In minutes, 459,000 cubic metres of water — equal to about 185 Olympic-sized swimming pools — surged down the valley. Within 20 minutes, the flood swept away homes, a school, and a clinic, altering 135 lives forever.

Just over two years later, on August 26, 2026, a far deadlier glacier collapse proved that Thame was not a freak accident. This disaster struck right where the western Hindu Kush meets the core Himalayan arc. This boundary matters deeply for our risk planning. The core Himalayas form the towering, steep barrier across India, Nepal, and Bhutan. The Hindu Kush stretches further west through Pakistan and Afghanistan. Together, they hold the largest reserve of ice outside the polar zones. Yet, their unique terrains face very different climate pressures. This recent collapse triggered massive, fast-moving flash floods down the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river valleys. The surge unleashed seismic energy equivalent to a 5.2-magnitude earthquake. As the torrent tore downstream, it claimed over 1,000 lives. It left thousands missing across the border region, including hundreds of foreign tourists and pilgrims.

The mountains are changing much faster than our ground systems can watch them.

To understand why these ice bombs are ticking, you have to look at how a glacial lake forms. Global temperatures are climbing. Glaciers across both the Hindu Kush and the Himalayas are melting at a rapid pace. As they shrink, they leave behind massive, deep pools of meltwater. These lakes are held back by nothing more than loose piles of rock, gravel, and ice. Experts call these unstable barriers moraines. Today, these fragile lakes number more than 25,000 across the region.

A recent UN-led study analysed nearly two centuries of mountain hazard data. The findings reveal a stark structural problem. China and Pakistan have recorded more individual lake bursts because their mountains are punishingly steep. However, India bears the absolute highest human toll, with 6,119 recorded fatalities. This vulnerability is entirely structural. Our downstream valleys are some of the most crowded and heavily developed areas on earth. Globally, about 15 million people live directly in the path of a potential GLOF. More than half of that exposed population lives in just four countries: India, Pakistan, China, and Peru.

The physics of these events leaves zero margin for error. A collapsing ice cliff or a sudden rockfall shifts the lake instantly. The resulting wave can break a moraine dam in seconds. Once that barrier fails, the water does not just flow down. It tears at the valley walls, picking up mud, heavy sediments, and giant boulders. By the time it hits a town, it has turned into a thick, heavy, moving entity possessing the force of an explosion. During the Thame disaster, the deluge travelled so fast that a satellite image taken just three hours prior showed absolutely no sign of danger.

Behind these dense statistics are the raw human stories of broken mountain life. For indigenous communities, like the Sherpas of Thame, a GLOF does not only destroy brick buildings. It also washes away centuries of cultural identity and traditional farming. It erases ancestral knowledge tied to the soil. The aftermath also leaves pristine forests and once-fertile fields buried under a sterile desert of grey mud and stone.

This hyper-rapid, unexpected nature of modern flooding rewrites the rules of climate risk. We can no longer build safety policies around old weather patterns. Traditional, ground-based monitoring alone cannot save a valley when a disaster strikes out of nowhere. Therefore, our basic definition of preparedness has to change.

Protecting these vulnerable populations demands a fundamental bridge between traditional mountain tracking and advanced space technology. The triggers are invisible from the ground; so we must make them visible from above. Moving from reactive disaster response to proactive, data-driven climate resilience is no longer an academic talking point. It is a race against time to disarm the ticking ice bombs hovering over our river valleys and cities.

Farhat Rafiq is Catastrophe Modeller, Climate and Risk Analyst, Geospatial Expert and formerly Director, Insurance Operating Unit, Moody’s, Delhi. Shivaji Bhandarkar is with the Department of Automobile Engineering and Environmental Science, Guru Gobind Singh Indraprastha University, and Department of Training and Technical Education, Government of NCT of Delhi

editorials.title: A fable's echoes
editorials.passage:
There is a persistent literary rumour that Jean de La Fontaine’s The Grasshopper and the Ant was more than a moral tale about thrift and idleness. Cultural critics have suggested that La Fontaine, writing during the reign of Louis XIV, was subtly commenting on a kingdom that could mobilise enormous resources for grand projects while ordinary people bore the costs. Whether or not the fable was aimed at the diversion of the Eure River to feed the fountains of Versailles, the allegory remains remarkably relevant to contemporary debates on water, power, and development.

The Yettinahole project in Karnataka provides a striking modern echo. In La Fontaine’s fable, the ant represents planning, accumulation, and the disciplined management of scarce resources. The grasshopper lives in the moment, enchanted by immediate desires and splendid possibilities. The tale is usually read as a lesson in personal responsibility. But read politically, it becomes a question of public priorities.

The Yettinahole project was conceived as a solution to water scarcity in Karnataka’s drought-prone eastern regions. Its promise is seductive. Divert west-flowing water from the Western Ghats, carry it across river basins, and quench the thirst of towns and villages in the eastern belt.

Yet critics have long argued that the project resembles the logic of Versailles more than the wisdom of the ant. Like the grand hydraulic ambitions of 17th-century France, the Yettinahole proposal carries the triumph of engineering imagination. It seeks to overcome geography itself, lifting and channeling water across ecological boundaries. The political appeal is obvious: large infrastructure projects are visible, dramatic, and symbolically powerful. But is the project solving a problem, or merely relocating ecological costs? The streams identified under Yettinahole are not isolated resources waiting to be harvested. They form part of a larger hydrological system feeding the Netravathi basin, sustaining ecosystems, agriculture, and communities downstream. Critics warn that diverting water from one region to satisfy another risks treating complex ecological relationships as engineering inconveniences.

Here the fable acquires new meaning. The true ant is not necessarily the government building pipelines and pumping stations in the name of water conservation. The true ant may be the watershed itself — the forests, soils, wetlands, and river systems that have stored water through centuries of ecological labour. The Western Ghats gather rainfall, release it gradually, and support an intricate web of life. To draw heavily from that account without fully understanding its limits is to mistake stored capital for disposable income.

The grasshopper, by contrast, is not a lazy individual but a development model that assumes every shortage can be solved by a larger diversion, a higher dam, a longer pipeline. This is not an argument against helping water-scarce regions. But there is a profound difference between solving a problem and postponing it. Investing in local watershed restoration, groundwater recharge, rainwater harvesting, urban demand management, and agricultural efficiency may lack the drama of a mega-project. But they are the work of ants: patient, decentralised, and often invisible.

The Yettinahole project confronts Karnataka with a similar dilemma. Should public policy celebrate mastery over nature, or work with natural systems to strengthen resilience? Should development be measured by the scale of infrastructure, or by the sustainability of outcomes?

La Fontaine’s genius was that he compressed political wisdom into the simplest of stories. The lesson was never merely about saving for winter. It was about understanding limits.

The ant would counsel otherwise: it would ask how much resilience can be preserved for tomorrow. In an age of climate uncertainty, that may be the most important question of all.

Nandini Hebbar teaches at MICA, Ahmedabad, and has authored the book, Gender, Caste and Class in South India’s Technical Institutions

editorials.title: Delicate test: Editorial on Indus Waters Treaty and India's stand against PCA ruling
editorials.passage:
India has, unsurprisingly, rejected the ruling this week of the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague in Pakistan’s favour over New Delhi’s decision to effectively suspend its participation in the Indus Waters Treaty. India, which decided that it could not continue to uphold the Indus pact after the April 2025 terror attack in Pahalgam, has consistently held that it does not recognise the jurisdiction of the PCA over the treaty. Indeed, it did not even participate in the hearings that culminated in the court’s interim verdict on Monday. As a repeated victim of Pakistani terrorism, India has legitimate grievances and is justified in making it clear — to Islamabad and the world — that business as usual cannot continue. It is equally true that the PCA is not a United Nations agency and ignoring its rulings does not amount to any disrespect to the UN system that India wants a bigger say in.

Yet, the true import of the PCA’s ruling extends beyond the Indus Waters Treaty. It poses a test to New Delhi’s avowed commitment to international institutions and to its own vulnerabilities over water security in a region where it is both an upper riparian state and a lower riparian nation. India must weigh its criticism of the PCA against the risk of damage to its standing as a nation that respects the international order. There is an additional irony. If India had never recognised the PCA as a legitimate body, its response to the Indus Waters Treaty would not have raised any eyebrows. But India had in July 2014 — under Prime Minister Narendra Modi — accepted the same court’s ruling against New Delhi, and in favour of Dhaka, in a maritime dispute. The PCA gave Bangladesh a bulk of the waters of the Bay of Bengal, while demarcating the maritime boundary between the neighbours. That approach has helped India distinguish itself from China, which, in 2016, rejected the PCA’s verdict against Beijing and in favour of the Philippines amid a dispute over the South China Sea. India must avoid creating the perception that New Delhi, like Beijing, remains impervious to the opinions of and verdicts delivered by international bodies. India must also remember that the same water weapon it can wield against Pakistan — however justified it may be — also leaves it vulnerable to similar threats from upper riparian neighbours, including China. India must seek to punish Pakistan but must not punish itself in the process.

editorials.title: Final whistle: Editorial on Lionel Messi’s extraordinary footballing legacy
editorials.passage:
Lionel Messi’s retirement from international football leaves the game poorer in terms of magic and his legion of fans forlorn. This is because in a career spanning over two decades, the Argentinian legend had cast a spell on connoisseurs and pundits alike of the beautiful game. The facts confirm his wizardry. In the 34 matches he played across six editions of the World Cup — football’s premier tournament — he scored 21 goals. Astonishingly, the majority of these goals — 15 — took place in the last two tournaments when ‘La Pulga’, as the player is called affectionately in Spanish, was not quite young. In these eight years, Argentina, shepherded by Mr Messi, won one World Cup and lost in the final of the other. This is a testament to the fact that like the finest of wines, Mr Messi has aged well as a player. His performance at the club level was as impressive. At Barcelona, he scored 672 goals in over 700 matches apart from making countless assists and lifted 35 trophies with the Catalan side. This list includes 10 La Liga trophies as well as four UEFA Champion Leagues.

Two elements remain integral to Mr Messi’s glittering legacy. Football has changed in terms of character, strategy and tactical systems employed by coaches. Many of these transitions have taken place within Mr Messi’s footballing career. Yet, he is one of those rare players who not only fits into nearly every conceivable tactical plan but also makes sure that a system works around him. The last gift bore dividends for Argentina in recent times when its coach favoured an approach that let Mr Messi be the glue around which the team played. This, in turn, challenges another commonly held assumption about the game: that of football being a team sport. It certainly is; but at times, an individual of prodigious talent, such as Mr Messi, can eclipse or be synonymous with an entire team. All this naturally leads to that question that is inevitably raised during many an adda — is Lionel Messi the greatest footballer ever? This debate cannot exclude Diego Maradona or Pele; neither can it be easily resolved. Perhaps it would be fair to conclude that football will remain indebted to this league of superlative players.

editorials.title: When life policy changes hands
editorials.passage:
Around seventy non-resident Indians, most of them in the Gulf, are putting together complaints against an Indian bank’s Dubai operations. Between 2017 and 2019 they were sold units in a Luxembourg fund that buys life insurance policies from Americans who no longer want them, pays the premiums, and collects the claim when the insured dies. They say it was described to them as capital protected, and that they were encouraged to borrow three to five times the money they had placed with the bank. The fund stopped returning money in 2020. The bank says, it only facilitated the investments, and that the fund’s performance was the fund house’s responsibility.

Whatever the regulators eventually conclude, the arrangement that failed there has a close Indian cousin, and our law has left it in an unusual position.

Strip the geography away. A company buys a man’s life insurance policy from him and he takes cash today. The company pays his premiums from then on, and when the claim falls due the money goes to the company rather than to his family. Its profit is the gap between what it pays and what it finally receives. Indian law calls it an absolute assignment which passes the policyholder’s rights under the policy to the buyer, subject to the terms of the policy and of the assignment itself. The company funds itself by promising outside investors a fixed return out of a payment whose timing is a death.

Sales of this kind are still few in India. The pool they draw on is very large. IRDAI figures placed before Parliament on August 3, 2026, show surrenders and withdrawals rising steadily over five years, and exceeding, for the first time in recent years, what insurers paid on policies that ran to maturity. How many of those policyholders sell rather than surrender is unknown, because nobody counts assignments made for money. The new reporting duty would produce that count for the first time.

India has been here before. In 2003 LIC found its policies being bought and sold like shares and told its offices to refuse such assignments. The courts ruled against it; the Supreme Court held in December 2015 that LIC had written the contract itself and could have barred assignment in it. Parliament had already acted: the amendment of 2015 rewrote Section 38 of the Insurance Act to let an insurer refuse an assignment that is not genuine, is against the policyholder’s or the public interest, or is meant for trading in the policy.

Four risks are worth setting out plainly, because no advertisement will.

First, the nominee. An absolute assignment cancels the nomination. The family that believes it is still covered is no longer the party the insurer will pay.

Second, the price. A buyer may offer a little more than the surrender value, which is what makes the offer attractive to a man who needs money. Set against that, he hands over the maturity amount and the death claim, keeping only cover that runs on without further premium. Cash today is bought at a heavy price in what is given up tomorrow.

Third, who gains from an early death. An investor promised a fixed return out of a death claim earns it faster the sooner the insured dies, and loses ground every month another premium goes out. Nobody has to behave badly for that to be true; it is how the arrangement is built. Insurance law has always required the buyer of a policy to have an interest in the life continuing. Here that interest runs the other way. India tests it once, when the policy is taken, and nothing tests it again when the policy changes hands. American regulators drew that line explicitly. Model laws issued there in 2007 prohibit a policy taken out at the very start for an investor’s benefit, while leaving alone the resale of a policy its owner already held. Twenty-nine States have since legislated to that effect.

Fourth, what happens if people live longer than expected. Premiums keep going out while the claims recede. A fund promising investors a fixed return, while its costs depend on when strangers die, has nothing to fall back on. The Luxembourg fund stopped returning money in 2020 after a rush of requests to withdraw, which is how the strain in such an arrangement shows itself.

Insurance companies are watched by IRDAI, and the trusteeship companies holding the policies by SEBI. However, the actual middleman who buys policies from needy people for cash falls into a legal gap that neither regulator directly oversees.

Even though the life insurance policy remains active and protected by insurance rules, the actual deal where the policyholder sells it for cash falls completely outside the law. The unregulated middleman buying the policy steps in when the policyholder is in urgent need of money — the precise moment when they are most vulnerable to being taken advantage of.

The Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Act, 2025 took effect on February 5, 2026, and is the widest rewriting of Indian insurance law since the sector opened. Section 38 was left untouched. The same Act widened the list of who counts as an insurance intermediary and empowered the regulator to add to it by notification, made it an offence to act as an intermediary without registering, and required insurers to record every assignment and report it to IRDAI on a concurrent basis. The regulator now has a basis to see the patterns and act on them. What is missing is the decision to treat these buyers as a regulated category at all.

Banning such assignments outright is the wrong instrument, and the Supreme Court has explained why. Public policy, it observed, is an unruly horse, and courts should be slow to ride it into private contracts. Regulation of this kind builds markets as often as it restricts them, and a policyholder who understands the bargain may still choose to make it.

First, IRDAI should specify the grounds on which an insurer may decline under Section 38(2). Parliament gave insurers that power in 2015 and it has gone unused, because trading is nowhere defined and a refusal invites litigation. A circular defining trading would let insurers refuse what Parliament has already empowered them to refuse.

Second, IRDAI should bring the buyers who remain within the regulated fold, leaving out banks that take a policy as security, employers, trustees and family arrangements. Each of those has an interest in the life continuing, and a buyer paying cash for the death claim holds the opposite one. That is the line, and it is Parliament’s own. Section 39 already treats a policy pledged as security differently from one bought outright, and restores the nomination once the loan is repaid. Registration would bring capital requirements, rules of conduct, disclosure and a grievance machinery.

Third, no insurer should register such a sale without a signed statement, in the policyholder’s own language, telling him who will now receive the death claim, what the maturity amount he gives up is worth, and what he gets in return. One notification and one form.

The Gulf investors are learning what happens when a product is sold across a regulatory boundary and nobody on either side owns the outcome. India need not wait for its own version to freeze before deciding who supervises

Kumar is former Managing Director, and Sudhakar is the former Executive Director, at LIC. Views are personal. All data are drawn from publicly available sources

editorials.title: Census, and tricky issues in recording caste
editorials.passage:
Now that the house-listing operations for the much-delayed Population Census have been completed and the population enumeration is eagerly awaited, the announcement that the Census questionnaire is being pilot-tested has come as something of a surprise. Unfortunately, little is known about its proposed contents.

More seriously, press reports have quoted senior officials as saying that caste will be recorded simply as reported by the respondent. This raises fundamental questions about both the feasibility of counting castes and the utility of the data so generated. Such a decision would be particularly disturbing when the disastrous experience of the Socio-Economic and Caste Census (SECC) 2011 is still fresh in our minds.

The accuracy of any census count requires that the item being counted be clearly identifiable. In an exercise as vast as the Indian population Census, it is, therefore, essential that the items included in the questionnaire are standardised, readily understood and capable of being recorded without ambiguity. A sample survey offers greater flexibility because enumerators can probe individual responses in greater detail. A Census, by contrast, must depend on uniform concepts and standardised procedures across the country to be adopted by millions of enumerators.

Normally, Census questionnaires are subjected to extensive technical scrutiny, giving users some indication of the concepts and definitions underlying the resulting data. When the 2021 Census was announced, for instance, there was no proposal to include a caste question in the Census schedule. There was, however, an announcement that the National Population Register would be updated alongside the Census, paving the way for the preparation of a National Register of Citizens. The chronology of these operations, as described by the Home Minister, generated considerable informed public debate.

The operationalisation of a caste question poses a major technical challenge. The experience of the SECC 2011 is a stark warning. Its caste data could not be satisfactorily tabulated, largely because caste names were not standardised and there was no comprehensive list against which responses could be classified. The exercise reportedly generated millions of caste and community names, making meaningful aggregation at the State level — and still more at the national level — virtually impossible.

The old Census reports provide ample evidence of the difficulties that arise when caste is left entirely to the respondent’s description. Recent caste surveys conducted by States such as Bihar and Telangana followed a different approach by providing a framework for classification. Yet these experiences cannot simply be transplanted to a national census. A State-level census can restrict its classification to castes found within that State. A national census cannot do so because of India’s substantial inter-State migration.

In Bihar, reported caste names were matched against a State master list of 214 unique castes. In Telangana, caste and sub-caste names were recorded along with the caste category used by the government. In either approach, however, migrants belonging to communities recognised in another State but absent from the local list could become problematic. They risk being classified as “others”, losing the identity necessary for meaningful national aggregation.

The problem is not merely hypothetical. Delhi has a substantial Scheduled Caste population but, according to the Census, no officially recognised Scheduled Tribe population, since the recognition of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes is State-specific. Yet the 2011-12 National Sample Survey estimated roughly half a million Scheduled Tribe persons in Delhi. Many were migrants from States where their tribal status is recognised. If a national caste census relies primarily on State-specific lists, such inter-State migrants could easily disappear into an amorphous “others” category. The problem would be particularly acute in States and cities experiencing large-scale immigration.

The preparation of these lists is, however, the critical task. The caste lists used in the 1931 Census, official documentation of castes and communities undertaken in the 1980s and documentation of the Socially and Educationally Backward Classes provide useful starting points. But no existing list can simply be adopted mechanically. Extensive consultation will be necessary to resolve differences in nomenclature, synonyms, sub-castes and claims of inclusion or exclusion.

This would take time — perhaps a few months — but such a preparation is indispensable if the caste census is to produce data of analytical and policy value. A technically rushed census may generate an enormous volume of information while failing to produce relevant statistics.

The historical experience of the Census illustrates why conceptual clarity matters. The 1931 Census, for instance, faced difficulties in defining the category of “Anglo-Indian”, then an influential community. The Travancore Census report noted that, in the 1921 Census, some English-speaking Christians who adopted European modes of dress had been included in the category, apparently without justification. A more precise definition was subsequently adopted based on ancestry in the male line. Understandably, the new definition resulted in considerable number of people being excluded. The episode illustrates a perennial census dilemma: a category cannot be completely open-ended and simultaneously remain statistically comparable.

Caste Census today presents complex conceptual and administrative problems. What is to be recorded when a respondent gives a broad caste category, a sub-caste, a community name, a local synonym or a caste name used in another State? How are overlapping names to be classified? How should claims that one caste is equivalent to, or distinct from, another be treated? These questions need to be settled before enumeration begins, not after millions of responses have been collected.

There is also an important question about the placement of the caste question in the questionnaire. Putting it at the beginning may influence responses to subsequent socio-economic questions, with respondents potentially interpreting their economic and social circumstances through the lens of caste. The ordering of questions, therefore, deserves careful consideration. Significantly, caste was placed at the end of the questionnaire in the 1931 Census.

The repeated changes in the timing of the Population Census, uncertainty about its coverage and continuing ambiguity about the eventual use of its data have already undermined confidence in one of India’s most important statistical exercises. The Census should not become an exercise driven by political compromise and expediency at the expense of technical rigour.

If the caste question is to be included, the opportunity should demonstrate precisely the opposite: that a politically sensitive exercise can be designed with the highest standards of statistical and administrative ingenuity.

Mohanan is former Chairman, Kerala State Statistical Commission; Kundu is Senior Fellow at IORA Ecological Solutions
