editorials.title: The changing economics of weak monsoon
editorials.passage:
Conventional wisdom suggests that a deficient monsoon weakens rural demand. This year may prove otherwise. Despite rains at 11-13 per cent below normal so far this season, sowing has better-than-expected, and even if weaker rains ultimately lower yields, rural demand seems to be better insulated than in past episodes of truant monsoons. Four years of favourable monsoons, expanding irrigation, lower inflation and a wider fiscal safety net are likely to have altered the transmission of a rainfall shock to the rural economy.

Almost three months into the south-west monsoon, rainfall remains broadly consistent with forecasts of a below-normal season, though its distribution has been uneven. A severely deficient June was followed by a stronger-than-expected July before rainfall weakened again in August, reflecting the combined influence of an emerging El Niño, a less supportive Indian Ocean Dipole and intermittent weather depressions. Spatial disparities have been pronounced too. Forecasts continue to point to a below-normal season.

Yet, contrary to what such an uneven monsoon might suggest, the rainfall shock has not translated into a major acreage shock. Overall sowing stands at 92 per cent of normal area and 90 per cent of last year’s level. Sowing has already been completed for maize, groundnut, sugarcane and jute and mesta. Sowing data was until mid-August and lagging crops such as cotton, bajra, tur, jowar, rice and soybean would stage some catch up over the remainder of August, provided soil moisture conditions remain supportive.

Why, then, has the monsoon shock not become a sowing shock? Early evidence suggests adaptation has played an important role. Cropping decisions appear to have responded to local soil moisture conditions, intermittent improvements in rainfall and State-level advisories. Water-intensive crops such as rice and sugarcane recovered in July after a dry June, although progress moderated again as rainfall weakened in August.

Groundnut illustrates the adjustment process well. All-India sowing, initially 42 per cent below last year’s level in June, subsequently recovered and moved above last year’s level.

Deficient rainfall initially restrained groundnut sowing in Gujarat even as Rajasthan advanced. Better rainfall in July supported recovery in Gujarat, while progress in Rajasthan moderated as deficits emerged there. More recently, abundant rainfall in Gujarat has encouraged additional acreage, with State data indicating sowing above normal levels.

Adaptation is also evident in State-level advisories, which have encouraged short-duration crops such as maize, bajra and moong in rain-stressed areas. This suggests the first transmission channel, from deficient rainfall to lower sowing, is weaker than expected. The risk has shifted instead to yields, particularly for less irrigated crops.

Increasingly, the key question is how well crops can withstand deficient rainfall when irrigation support is limited. Crop vulnerability depends on rainfall deficits and irrigation coverage. Better-irrigated crops can withstand weaker rains, while others remain exposed. Among crops showing relatively robust sowing progress, sugarcane is almost entirely irrigated even though some major producing States face rainfall deficits.

By contrast, irrigation coverage for maize is considerably lower in several key producing States that are also experiencing rainfall weakness. Similar concerns arise for tur, where irrigation coverage remains limited and sowing is already lagging.

Crisil’s Deficient Rainfall Impact Parameter (DRIP) assigns the highest vulnerability to tur, followed by jowar, bajra, maize, soybean and cotton. The implication is clear: the monsoon shock may yet become a yield shock even if it has not become a sowing shock. This distinction matters because weaker yields can depress output and kharif-driven incomes.

A yield shock though is unlikely to translate proportionately into a rural demand shock. Rural households are less dependent on crop incomes than in the past. Livestock, fisheries and forestry provide an important income buffer because they are less exposed to weather stress. Moreover, the rural economy enters this period of uncertainty from a position of strength. Good rains in recent years would have supported farm output and incomes while strengthening household balance sheets. Low inflation has provided additional relief.

Consequently, the impact of one weak monsoon year may be absorbed rather than amplified. State advisories have also promoted short-duration and drought-resilient crops such as pulses, millets and oilseeds that perform better under moisture stress. Meanwhile, irrigation coverage has expanded to about 60 per cent of net sown area in fiscal 2025 from 48.8 per cent in fiscal 2016, providing an additional layer of resilience.

Policy support offers a further buffer, particularly for vulnerable households. Cash transfer schemes now operate in 17 States and provide a median monthly benefit of ₹1,500 to low-income households.

Our estimates suggest this covers about 74 per cent of monthly expenditure in rural areas.

PM-KISAN provides eligible farmers with ₹6,000 annually through direct benefit transfers. Together with free and subsidised foodgrain programmes and GST reductions on mass-consumption items, these measures have strengthened rural household balance sheets. As a result, a moderate decline in crop income need not translate into an equivalent fall in rural consumption.

To conclude, a below-normal and uneven monsoon need not result in a significant rural demand shock.

The experience also underlines the importance of structurally monsoon-proofing rural India. Irrigation coverage has expanded steadily, supported by higher government capital expenditure, and accelerating this process will be critical to limit income and food-price vulnerability to rainfall fluctuations, reduce import dependence in select crops and strengthen India’s long-term agricultural export potential.

At the same time, the rising contribution of allied agricultural activities is providing a natural hedge against weather shocks. Continued policy efforts to strengthen these sectors can further support rural incomes.

The weakness in this year’s monsoon cannot be ignored, but one poor rainfall season need not undo the resilience rural India has built. But if rainfall deficiencies deepen and linger, the strain could extend into the winter crop, weakening those buffers and placing broader pressure on incomes and demand.

The writer is Principal Economist and Senior Director at Crisil Ltd. Views are personal

editorials.title: Coop banks in transition
editorials.passage:
The RBI on August 5, 2026 released the “Draft Guidelines for ‘on tap’ Licensing of Urban Co-operative Banks” for public/stakeholders’ comments. The Draft Guidelines (DGs) specify stringent conditions for co-operative societies to apply for Urban Co-operative Bank (UCB) licences.

The RBI Governor’s October 2025 Monetary Policy Statement proposed to publish a Discussion Paper (DP) on licencing of new UCBs. Although since 2004 the UCB licensing was paused, the sector had progressed well during the subsequent two decades. Therefore, the stakeholders were demanding to restore the licencing process.

The DP, published in January 2026, recommended several tough conditions for licencing new UCBs.

Prior to the DP, an RBI screening committee in 2001 had recommended that it should be made mandatory for all new UCBs to come into being through a process of graduation from a CCS on the strength of proven and verifiable track records.

This was further supported by the Expert Committee on Licensing of New Urban Co-operative Banks (2011) (Chairman: Y H Malegam) and the High Powered Committee on Urban Co-operative Banks (2015) (Chairman: R Gandhi).

Therefore, there was a compelling need to make available, on tap, strict licencing norms for the CCSs aspiring to become UCBs so that the latter remains, ab initio, strong, well-diversified and immune to failure.

It is noteworthy here that UCBs are evidenced to be more fragile than the commercial banks.

The entry norms, as briefly mentioned below, mostly follow the DP’s recommendations.

Eligibility: CCSs in existence for at least 10 years.

Minimum Capital and Other Requirements: The CCS should have a deposit size of at least ₹10,000 crore and minimum net worth of at least ₹300 crore (as per audited financials at March-end of the previous financial year of application). [At March-end 2024 (latest available), only 6 out of 49 Scheduled UCBs had deposits above ₹10,000 crore.]

Registration: In the initial phase, the MSCCSs will be considered.

Track Record: The CCS must demonstrate a positive and progressive trend in operating and financial parameters in the previous five years. The Capital to Risk-Weighted Assets Ratio should not be less than 12 per cent, and the Net Non-Performing Assets ratio should not be more than three per cent at March-end of the previous financial year of application.

Fit and Proper: No member should have a shareholding of over five per cent. The RBI would assess the ‘fit and proper’ status of the Board of Directors.

Lack of a comprehensive, credible and up-to-date financial database of CCSs in the public domain restricts us to say how many, or which ones, would be eligible for UCB application. Even if some are eligible, whether their members would be willing is a big question. A bigger question is whether their applications would pass the RBI’s litmus test.

If no single CCS is eligible, some CCSs would like to merge themselves to improve their financials to meet the RBI benchmarks. Thus, a ‘churn’ in the CCS segment may ensue.

Whether individually or through mergers, the aspirational UCBs would like to improve their operations and financials with a view to meeting the RBI stipulations at a future date. In other words, the DGs would be a ‘challenge’ for them and in this sense, serve as a ‘wake-up’ call for CCSs to ‘sanitize’ themselves.

The new UCBs cannot pay their depositors the high rates of interest as they used to do as CCSs. This may trigger inter-CCS deposit ‘flight.’ However, the CCS depositors should be happy that their deposits in the new UCB will be fully protected up to the prevailing deposit insurance limit.

On the assets side, the new UCBs cannot deploy their lendable resources in any sector and at any rate.

Together the above two will disincentivise aggressive depositors/members of CCSs to vote for UCB conversion.

In order to survive in the modern day banking the new UCBs have to invest in skilled manpower, especially those with knowledge on banking, accountancy, IT, compliance, cross-selling, etc. For this purpose, besides fresh recruitment, they may have to poach the existing UCBs – both necessitating payment of market-determined pay packages.

Similarly, acquisition of appropriate IT systems is crucial, particularly when the IT environment is constantly mutating and ensuring cybersecurity has emerged as a major challenge even for the large commercial banks. The new UCBs have to continuously invest in IT empowerment.

Last but not least, corporate governance, which has proved to be the Achilles’ heel in the case of several banking crises, has to be given the pride of place. Therefore, the ‘fit and proper’ test should aim at critical qualitative evaluation of the members of the Board as well as other critical areas of management.

All said, it is felt that new UCB applications would trickle in in the medium-term, even though the final guidelines come out in one or two months.

Das is a former Assistant General Manager (Economist), SBI. Rath is a former central banker

editorials.title: Rethinking the way we work
editorials.passage: India is at an inflection point when it comes to the future of work. The country has the talent, ambition and digital momentum to become one of the world’s most AI-enabled economies. But the bigger opportunity is not simply to adopt AI. It is to fundamentally redesign how work gets done. For years, digital transformation has focused on putting technology around existing processes. AI gives organisations an opportunity to rethink those processes from the ground up: how people find information, make decisions, collaborate, develop skills and spend their time. The signals from India’s workforce are already compelling. Recent workforce research finds that 89% of employees say AI improves their work experience, while 32% say AI is already embedded in core workflows. Yet 56% say they spend at least half their effort translating and coordinating across systems. These numbers tell us something important. Employees are ready for AI, and organisations are beginning to integrate it. But there is still a significant gap between having AI available and redesigning work around it. Closing this gap will be one of the defining opportunities of the next decade. ALSO READA smarter return to work Why India’s AI opportunity goes beyond automation Recent research shows that 56% of Indian employees spend at least half their effort on manual handoffs between systems and teams, rather than creating value. When I speak with business and HR leaders across India, the conversation has moved beyond whether AI will transform work. The focus is now on where AI can remove friction, create more time for meaningful work, build future-ready skills and strengthen trust. India’s next phase of AI adoption must go beyond adding more tools and instead focus on redesigning work itself. That means connecting systems, eliminating unnecessary coordination and enabling people to focus on higher-value, human-led work. More than a third of Indian employees lose over seven hours a week simply moving information between systems, compared with a global average of 21%. That is effectively a full working day spent on coordination rather than value creation. This is more than a productivity challenge; it is a workforce transformation opportunity. The government’s IndiaAI Mission recognises that opportunity by combining AI infrastructure with FutureSkills and industry collaboration. The next phase of AI must therefore move beyond automating individual tasks. By embedding intelligence into workflows, organisations can eliminate friction, return time to employees and enable people to focus on judgement, creativity and innovation. That is the real promise of AI: not simply faster work, but better work. Skills, not just jobs, will define the next workforce The future of work will be shaped less by which jobs AI replaces and more by which skills it makes more valuable. Research on the evolving workplace finds that 43% of Indian employees use both AI tools mandated by their employers and additional tools they choose themselves. ALSO READThe next leap: The biggest gains will come from execution from AI This signals a workforce actively exploring how AI can augment its capabilities. It also makes skills development a strategic priority. For India, AI can help organisations identify adjacent skills, personalise learning and create pathways to higher-value roles. This can turn workforce transformation into continuous capability building. Instead of treating skills as static credentials attached to particular roles, businesses will need to understand how capabilities evolve and where employees can move as technology changes the nature of work. The CHRO as architect of an AI-powered enterprise AI is redefining the role of HR from workforce management to workforce architecture. Leaders need real-time visibility into critical skills, emerging capabilities and where technology can augment people. AI enables continuous workforce planning, helping organisations respond faster to changing business priorities. For them, this agility can become a powerful competitive advantage. Trust will be the foundation of successful AI adoption. Around 95% of Indian employees say AI increases their confidence in decisions when they trust the underlying system and data. This makes the quality, security and integrity of enterprise data as important as AI capability itself. As AI moves deeper into workflows, organisations must combine transparency, strong governance and human oversight. Employees need to understand not only what AI can do, but also how decisions are made, what data is being used and where human judgement remains essential. The future will not be humans versus machines, but humans and AI working together, combining AI’s ability to analyse and automate with human judgement, creativity, empathy and accountability. India’s opportunity is bigger than AI adoption India’s opportunity is not simply to adopt AI, but to redefine how work gets done. Research shows that only 32% of Indian employees say AI is deeply embedded in their organisation’s core workflows, highlighting the significant opportunity ahead. India’s broader technology ecosystem is already moving towards this next phase. The IndiaAI Mission is bringing together government, industry and academia to strengthen AI infrastructure, skills and innovation. For enterprises, the next step is to move beyond standalone AI tools and redesign workflows around human and machine strengths. That means connecting systems, reducing unnecessary handoffs, building skills continuously and putting trust at the centre of deployment. India has the opportunity to lead this shift. Its advantage will not come simply from adopting AI faster, but from using it to create organisations where technology removes friction and people have more time to do the work that matters. The writer is president – India, Workday, a cloud-based software company. editorials.title: Ben-Gvir posts Palestinians on conveyor belts to detention camps. The world is silent
editorials.passage:
L et me introduce you to Itamar Ben-Gvir, the leader of Israel’s far-right Jewish Power (Otzma Yehudit) party, the minister of national security, and an almost cartoonishly evil man. You’ll have heard his name before: he made international news when he filmed himself taunting bound activists who had been detained trying to deliver humanitarian aid to Gaza. But you might not be familiar with many of his recent shocking comments, because they haven’t been widely covered by much of the US media.

Let’s start with an AI-generated video that Ben-Gvir posted on Twitter/X on Sunday and then deleted . It shows portly Palestinian prisoners being loaded on to a conveyor belt and going into a detention camp, then emerging emaciated. The caption is “we promised – we delivered!” which seems to be a reference to the national security minister’s promise to worsen conditions for Palestinian prisoners. An ambitious goal, considering conditions are already hellish: Israeli human rights group B’Tselem has likened the prisons where Palestinians are kept to “ torture camps ”.

I’m being diplomatic with my summary of this latest video, by the way. I suggest you go watch it yourself to fully take in how awful it is. (It may have been deleted, but it lives on online). If the podcaster Hasan Piker had tweeted something similar, with Israelis as the subject rather than Palestinians, it would be front-page news. US lawmakers, all of whom seem to be obsessed with Piker, would be demanding that the podcaster be punished.

Ben-Gvir, by the way, has some imaginative ideas for punishment. One of his sick fantasies is to put crocodiles in moats around prisons where Palestinians are held to stop prison breaks. The plan is now on hold because Israeli rights groups have said it is cruel to crocodiles.

I can’t stress enough that, in any discussion of Palestinian “prisoners”, it’s important to remember that many of these people have not gone through any sort of due process. Thousands of prisoners, including about 200 children , are held under “administrative detention”: a technocratic name for a dystopian practice.

To quote the B’Tselem definition : “In administrative detention, a person is held without trial without having committed an offense, on the grounds that he or she plans to break the law in the future. As this measure is supposed to be preventive, it has no time limit. The person is detained without legal proceedings, by order of the regional military commander, based on classified evidence that is not revealed to them.”

In other words: if you are Palestinian, heavily armed Israeli soldiers can come into your house in the middle of the night , drag you into a de facto torture chamber despite the fact that you haven’t committed a crime, and hold you there indefinitely without telling you why you’re being held or informing your family where you are.

When you hear the word “prisoner”, people like Ben-Gvir want you to think of dangerous terrorists who deserve everything they get. In reality, many are people like Layan Nasir: a 23-year-old woman who was taken away at gunpoint from her parents’ home for no clear reason and only made international news because she is a Christian.

But back to Ben-Gvir, who presides over prisoners. One of the minister of national security’s greatest achievements is a racist death penalty law that, because of the way it is worded, exclusively applies to Palestinians . Last month Ben-Gvir posted a video of a gallows complex where Palestinians convicted of terror offences will be hanged . For his birthday in June, he celebrated with a noose-themed cake .

Ben-Gvir doesn’t just want to hang his enemies; he wants more bloodshed in Gaza – which is still very much a killing field despite a so-called ceasefire. “I think we should be doing 30 to 40 targeted assassinations [in Gaza] per night,” Ben-Gvir recently said on a podcast. “Not just those who pose an immediate threat. There are people there who don’t deserve to live … They are not even people.”

I could go on and on: Ben-Gvir is a busy man. He recently filmed himself entering prison cells containing Palestinian women and taunting them. On the same podcast where he urged nightly killings in Gaza, he went on to say that he thought Israel should occupy the entirety of Gaza. And, on Monday, he stormed the al-Aqsa mosque compound in East Jerusalem, accompanied by extremist settlers and with the protection of the Israeli military.

This is something he does regularly: it is a blatant provocation and a contravention of an agreement that gives Muslims exclusive rights to worship at al-Aqsa while Jews pray at the Western Wall.

Ben-Gvir and others like him, however, want to change the decades-old status quo and have Israel control everything. “We are in charge here in Jerusalem and all of the land of Israel,” Ben-Gvir said during a 2023 visit to the compound.

Ben-Gvir is so shameless that there is no way to spin his conduct. He has been condemned and sanctioned by politicians and governments around the world. Nevertheless, Israel’s apologists have tried to cast him as a fringe figure. “Ben-Gvir’s statements do not reflect the policy of the State of Israel and should be condemned by all who care about Israel’s future,” the American Jewish Committee stated in August, after the politician’s comments about settlement in Gaza.

Some of Ben-Gvir’s peers have also tried to distance themselves from the extremist. The foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, condemned the video where Ben-Gvir taunts foreign activists saying : “You are not the face of Israel.”

Make no mistake: Ben-Gvir may be an embarrassment, but he is no anomaly. He is very much the face of modern Israel and his vision for the country accurately reflects the reality on the ground.

“Israeli policy is directed toward making life unbearable for Palestinians wherever they live, so that their emigration can be described as an act of free will,” the Israeli journalist Amira Hass wrote in Haaretz this week. “‘Erasure’ is the nightmare solution being written into reality every day.” Settler violence is escalating, more land in the West Bank and Gaza is being seized, and there has been widespread dehumanization of Palestinians in Israeli society .

Hass writes: “Together, these and similar forces are creating the material, ideological and psychological infrastructure within Israeli-Jewish society for another mass expulsion of Palestinians and for what might accompany it: mass slaughter.”

I’m quoting Hass because she is a brilliant journalist. But, I’ll be honest, I’m also quoting her because I’m part-Palestinian and she’s Israeli. I’m quoting Hass because, by virtue of being Israeli, she is seen as someone worth listening to. The world has made it very clear that it doesn’t want to listen to Palestinians, that we are barbarians who should not be believed.

And it is this sort of widespread dehumanization that has resulted in the complete shamelessness of a man like Ben-Gvir. He did not come into power in a vacuum: he was helped into his position by an international community which has afforded Israel complete impunity. He has been aided and abetted by international media organizations that have helped demonize Palestinians , cast doubt on our claims, and manufacture consent for erasure and expulsion.

He has been bolstered by lawmakers who tell us that we must defend Israel at all costs. And now, in the wasteland that is Gaza, in the nightly pogroms by Israeli settlers in the West Bank, and in Ben-Gvir’s brazen bloodlust, we are seeing the inevitable outcome of this unconditional support. Ben-Gvir is no aberration; he is the international community’s creation.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian US columnist

editorials.title: The people of France are in an extraordinary funk about their future – here’s why
editorials.passage:
F rance, as the French travel writer Sylvain Tesson once noted, “is a paradise inhabited by people who think they live in hell”. As the campaign for next year’s presidential election hits its stride with ever more wannabes declaring their candidacies, the country is in a particularly sullen mood.

If the vote were held now, the anti-immigration populist Marine Le Pen would have a strong chance of romping into the Élysée palace, riding a wave of voter disillusionment with the entire political class and a sense that “we’ve tried everything else”. But a lot can happen between now and 18 April 2027, the date of the first round. France is also a country of sudden shocks.

In spring 2011, Dominique Strauss-Kahn, the then head of the IMF and an admired former finance minister, was hot favourite to become the Socialist party candidate who would beat the incumbent conservative Nicolas Sarkozy in the 2012 race. But Strauss-Kahn was felled by a sexual harassment scandal and the unfancied socialist politician François Hollande ended up in the Élysée. In 2016, the former conservative prime minister François Fillon was well ahead in the race to succeed Hollande, then he was exposed as having arranged taxpayer-funded phoney parliamentary jobs for his wife. He finished third and a young centrist outsider without a party machine, Emmanuel Macron, went on to triumph.

To understand the backdrop to next year’s election – with huge stakes for Europe and the western alliance as well as for France – it’s worth examining the unique features that distinguish the French funk from the crisis facing other advanced democracies. After all, politics has become more raw and polarised in many countries. Other big European economies are stagnating. Mainstream parties are shrinking and fragmenting across Europe under growing challenges from insurgent rightwing national populists as well as a new radical, often ecologist, left. Political instability is accelerated everywhere by social-media frenzy and the 24/7 news cycle.

But several historical factors make the French malaise special, as I explored in a recent conversation with Michel Wieviorka, an eminent sociologist and author of numerous studies on French society, including Où va la France : Métamorphose ou Déchéance? (Where is France Headed: Metamorphosis or Decline?).

France was Europe’s first centralised state, with a culture of dirigiste economic development harking back to Cardinal Richelieu, Louis XIV and his minister Jean-Baptiste Colbert in the 17th century. That tradition was revived by Charles de Gaulle and postwar governments that used a powerful national economic planning commissariat to drive industrial modernisation, including the nuclear programme, the aerospace sector and massive public infrastructure investment.

This helps explain why French people have great expectations of the state and accept some of the highest levels of taxation, income redistribution and public spending as a proportion of economic output of any major economy. It also helps explain why France’s debt-to-GDP ratio of 118% is among the highest and fastest rising in Europe.

“The French are very attached to public services and anxious about their degradation, which is spectacular in public education but also in the justice system, the police, the tax system and health services, as revealed by the Covid-19 pandemic,” Wieviorka said. “They have the feeling that we used to be a great country at the forefront of modernity, but it is now falling apart.”

Another unique characteristic is a multi-century tradition of often violent protest. From the peasant jacqueries and Paris barricades of the 16th and 17th centuries to the landmark upheaval of the 1789 French revolution, revolt against authority has long been seen as legitimate by a large part of society. As Jean-Paul Sartre put it, “ It is right to rebel .” The French labour movement, too, was rooted in anarcho-syndicalism before being dominated by the communist party, and lacks the British or German trade unions’ tradition of reformist compromise.

Like the English did in the 17th century, the French executed their king in the 18th century, but it took almost another century to finally abolish monarchy after two royal restorations and two emperors. The French left fought for the republican principle, prevailing over authoritarian forces backed by the Catholic church in the Dreyfus affair at the end of the 19th century. That led to a strict separation of church and state and the principle of secularism that enjoys consensus support today.

However, as Wieviorka noted, the decline of France’s Christian identity and religious observance has coincided with the rise of Islam, mostly among people of immigrant origin. This has stirred anxieties fanned by mainstream conservative and hard-right politicians and the new-right media empire of the billionaire Vincent Bolloré .

These fears explain the rise of the extreme-right Front National founded by Jean-Marie Le Pen in 1972 , which Wieviorka called “the pioneering national-populist party in Europe”, putting the fight against immigration at the centre of its agenda. Rebranded in 2018 as the National Rally (RN) by his daughter, Marine, in a quest for respectability, the party has roots in the Vichy regime that collaborated with Nazi Germany but swapped antisemitism for anti-Islamism, advocating “national priority” for French citizens in welfare, housing and healthcare.

Another distinguishing feature is France’s political and administrative elite, rebuilt on meritocratic lines after the second world war with the creation of L’École nationale d’administration (ENA) to train top civil servants and captains of nationalised enterprises, many of whom made a career in politics. The system has become ossified and spawned a self-perpetuating elite – the so-called énarques – increasingly seen as remote from ordinary French people’s concerns.

These factors combined explain the state of public opinion on the eve of the campaign – deeply pessimistic about the state of the country, anxious about identity, declining public services and the cost of living, and disillusioned with a political establishment seen as having failed on all these fronts.

To Wieviorka’s matrix of factors underlying the political malaise, I would add a widespread lack of economic realism and a belief that what the French call “public money”, which in the UK or Germany is known as “taxpayers’ money”, is infinitely extendable.

Economic unrealism makes France particularly susceptible to magic money solutions such as RN’s fantasy that the debt and deficit would melt away if the government only stopped welfare payments to immigrants and slashed its EU contribution, or the radical leftist Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s claim that France just needs to write off “cost free” 18% of its debt held by the European Central Bank and confiscate all inheritances of more than €12m.

No wonder there’s little time for politicians who propose dreary real-world solutions such as raising the retirement age or curbing some welfare benefits. A famous slogan in the student uprisings of May 1968 proclaimed: “Be realistic, demand the impossible”. The big risk now is that the French vote with their gut rather than with their head. At a time of such geopolitical and fiscal peril for France and Europe, that is an alarming prospect.

Paul Taylor is a senior visiting fellow at the European Policy Centre

editorials.title: The wars in Ukraine and Iran are becoming dangerously enmeshed
editorials.passage:
R ussia hasn’t yet killed large numbers of Europeans outside Ukraine, but it’s getting closer. The night of 4-5 August, an airport bus driver discovered an armed drone lying near the tarmac of the Leipzig-Halle airport, which is a central hub of Europe’s logistical support to Ukraine’s war effort. A cargo jet, meanwhile, may have struck a second drone shortly after takeoff, forcing an abrupt landing, and investigators found a third drone laden with military explosives nearby.

In 2024, incendiary devices hidden in parcels ignited in DHL cargo at the same airport. Had these detonated in the air, a major air catastrophe and large-scale civilian casualties would have ensued, probably resulting in a broader war.

The most recent incident may be what prompted the CIA director, John Ratcliffe, to get on a plane for Moscow last week. There, according to reports, he warned his counterparts against attacks on Nato territory, urged them to curb support for Iran, argued that escalation in Ukraine would backfire, and pressed for a deal with Ukraine to end the war.

Ratcliffe’s trip is unlikely to have much impact on the Kremlin’s plans for an escalation against Ukraine in the coming months – but it is further evidence of the dangerous and growing enmeshment of the Iran and Ukraine wars.

Sending Ratcliffe to Moscow is a logical choice for the White House, given the substantial role the intelligence services play in Putin’s government and justifiable concern that he may be getting too-rosy assessments of the war from his own team. The attempt at diplomacy is to be applauded. Nevertheless, the Trump administration’s refusal to end the war with Iran is working at cross purposes with their effort to end the war in Ukraine. They are steering into the storm, not out of it.

One of the reasons for Ratcliffe’s visit to Moscow, according to the Washington Post, was to dispel the Kremlin’s belief that the Trump White House was distracted from Ukraine by Iran. Good luck with that. The reporting on the severe depletion of US interceptor stocks from the war on Iran is so extensive it can only have encouraged Vladimir Putin to launch even more deadly missile strikes against Ukraine’s defenseless population.

Ukraine, for its part, has sent 228 specialists and truckloads of drones to assist the Gulf states in their defense against Iranian missile strikes, prompting at least one Iranian lawmaker to declare Ukraine fair game for its own attacks. And Ukraine struck an Iranian commercial vessel in late July. Russia has meanwhile provided Iran with battlefield intelligence that make its strikes more deadly. Moscow has, of course, also long benefited from Iranian-designed drones to attack Ukraine.

Both conflicts are getting worse and going nowhere at the same time. True, Putin is in a pinch, with an economy badly damaged by Ukrainian strikes against Russian oil refineries and logistics hubs, but the pinch will just as easily prompt Russia’s leader toward escalation as it will restraint – especially if he sees the US distracted again in the Middle East and believes he has a window of opportunity to deal a crushing death blow to Kyiv.

Putin, like Zelensky, like Trump, and like the Iranian leadership, faces the same sunk-cost dilemma that has led so many of history’s wartime leaders to double down on fruitless military operations – from Alcibiades in Sicily, to Napoleon in Russia , to LBJ in Vietnam. If today’s leaders follow suit, the costs and escalation risks will mount while the conflicts fuse further.

Meanwhile, Xi Jinping and Putin met on Monday and will join Iran’s leaders in Bishkek this week for the annual summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization. They will discuss their plan to link their energy markets even more closely and probably condemn the new “economic offensive” that the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, announced last week to intensify pressure on Iran. Beijing may not want to see either war continue, but it also does not want to see Russia or Iran lose outright, and it is still in a strong position to avoid this outcome by helping the Iranians and Russians stave off the worst effects of the war on their economies and populations.

Ratcliffe’s trip was necessary, especially in light of Russia’s reckless grey-zone operations in Europe . But it will not be enough. His predecessor, Bill Burns, once went to Moscow in an effort to warn Russia against attacking Ukraine. That intervention fell on deaf ears, as Ratcliffe’s also will.

Clearer plans to end both wars through more positive inducements are badly needed.

To start, Washington should settle with Iran by unfreezing assets and offering sanctions relief in exchange for a real ceasefire and a framework arrangement for joint control of the strait by the littoral powers. It can then work to mitigate the consequences of this loss with a major push to diversify energy supplies – through alternative routes out of the region, alternative sources such as Venezuela, and a push on renewables. Ukraine, meanwhile, needs to become more serious about neutrality. It also needs a real debate about whether hanging on to the remainder of the Donbass it controls is worth indefinitely perpetuating the war.

In the conclusion to his recent book, The Coming Storm, which traces the parallels between today’s world and the world on the eve of the first world war, the historian Odd Arne Westad writes: “A key lesson of the world before 1914 is that regional conflicts, long left unresolved, can be the powder kegs that set off a global conflagration.” As the Iran and Ukraine conflicts intertwine without an end in sight, the world’s leaders should take such warnings far more seriously. But without real pressure from their citizens, they may not.

History is not doomed to repeat itself. But you don’t need to be a renowned historian to recognize the dangers the world is throwing up before us, nor to lament the failure of our leaders to calm these storms.

Christopher S Chivvis is a senior fellow and director of the American Statecraft Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. He served as the United States national intelligence officer for Europe from 2018 to 2021

editorials.title: China’s demise was gleefully predicted by the west – meanwhile, it built an AI revolution
editorials.passage:
A lmost from the moment it began, the end of the Chinese economic miracle has been much anticipated. Thick and fast, the books have come explaining how it will end badly. Overinvestment. A country wallowing in debt. The collapse of the property market . Political repression. The demand for democracy from a growing middle class. All have been put forward as reasons for the inevitable terminal crisis.

Even those impressed by the country’s rapid growth took comfort from the notion that the west would continue to dominate advanced manufacturing while China would be stuck assembling TVs. And while the wait for its much-predicted demise has gone on and on, China has become the workshop of the world.

This process has come in two distinct phases. Initially, it is true, there was a concentration on low-cost manufactured goods because cheap labour costs provided a competitive advantage. Firms left for east Asia in search of higher profits. Without China 1.0, Donald Trump would have remained a New York property developer and Brexit might never have happened.

Yet, the Chinese were not content to remain solely the producers of low-cost consumer goods and began to invest heavily in higher-end manufacturing. China 2.0 shattered the illusion that it would forever remain a developing economy destined to produce low-grade products and little else.

The market in solar panels was captured. It became the world leader in batteries and electric vehicles . It no longer has to import machine tools from Germany because it is now capable of making its own. The rise of the far-right Alternative für Deutschland is in no small measure due to the threat posed by China to German manufacturing jobs.

Of course, China’s critics have a point. The model relies too heavily on investment and has much excess capacity. The country produces far more goods than it can consume domestically, particularly given the low level of wages and a relatively ungenerous welfare system. As a result, China can only keep growing at a rate that prevents rising unemployment from leading to social unrest if it exports its surfeit of goods to the rest of the world. China found itself isolated at the recent meeting of finance ministers of the G20 group of leading developed and developing countries, facing criticism from all sides for failing to boost domestic demand for its products .

Perhaps this means the rest of the world has finally woken up to the threat. If it has, that would not be a moment too soon because China is now competing with the US for dominance in the race to develop artificial intelligence. Welcome to China 3.0.

In July, a Chinese startup called Moonshot unveiled its Kimi K3 model and it was an instant success. Just two days after its launch, the company suspended new subscriptions because demand was too great for its computing capacity. That was not surprising given that Kimi K3 was marketed as being able to match the models of its US rivals – such as the latest versions of OpenAI’s ChatGPT – at no cost. This was not a fluke or a random event.

As Edoardo Campanella of UniCredit notes, Beijing is pursuing a clear AI strategy: staying close to the technological frontier, diffusing its models throughout the global economy, and setting standards across international markets. “If this strategy succeeds, the third China shock might not just disrupt the global economy, but also the global balance of power ,” says Campanella.

Beijing’s strategy might not succeed but even so there are three things that are striking about the AI development race. The first is that this would appear to be the worst possible time for Washington to antagonise its traditional allies by whacking them with punitive tariffs. The US needs all the friends it can muster.

The second is that the arrival on the scene of free Chinese AI models could spell big trouble for global markets. Until now, the US has been confident its technological prowess will give it the upper hand in the AI development race and that has justified massive investment in technology companies.

Despite rising oil prices, share prices on Wall Street have reflected confidence not just that AI will transform economies but that the US will be the main beneficiary. But if China can develop its AI models at a lower cost and offer them for nothing, investors will soon start to question whether the massive investment in the US justifies the sky-high share prices of tech companies. China’s success in AI could prick the stock market bubble .

Finally, there are lessons that countries such as Britain need to learn from China if it is to re-industrialise. When China began to build up its manufacturing strength almost 50 years ago, it saw itself as a developing country. It had no illusions about the scale of the challenge but had a plan and stuck to it.

There was no aversion to picking winners. Nor would the strategy be left exposed to the whims of speculators. Instead, there was a willingness to use all the policy tools available: subsidies, tariffs, exchange controls and state investment.

The result is what we see now: a China that has shifted through the gears from an industrial policy dominated by cheap goods to an industrial policy of everything. Sure, China’s model has its flaws but there is a stark contrast with Britain’s negligent approach since the late 1970s. One country is serious about manufacturing and the other isn’t.

Larry Elliott is a Guardian columnist

editorials.title: I inadvertently misled parliament over a British nuclear scandal. Now I’m calling for justice
editorials.passage:
I n December 2018, as defence minister, I inadvertently misled parliament. Asked whether blood samples had been taken from service personnel for radiological monitoring during the nuclear bomb tests, I relayed the line provided to me by the Ministry of Defence: it was “unable to locate any information” suggesting blood samples had been taken for radiological monitoring at the tests.

I now know the reality was very different – these samples were taken across the armed services branches. But those veterans seeking compensation for serious illnesses developed after radiation exposure have been unable to access them. This is among the greatest scandals in Britain, and it must be addressed.

More than 20,000 armed forces personnel took part in dozens of nuclear tests and nearly 600 radiation experiments, the majority between 1952 and 1967. This was for the entirety of the cold war. The science was deemed necessary. How effective were our own bombs and, just as importantly, how well could our military function if the Soviet Union used theirs against us? Test after test was conducted in the Australian desert, at Christmas Island in the Pacific, and we also sent service personnel into the atomic clouds of allies and enemies. Yet their medical records for the period are missing.

Other nuclear nations, such as the US, France and the Soviet Union, did the same. Yet they acknowledged that it happened and created dedicated compensation schemes for nuclear test veterans who subsequently developed serious illnesses. Britain stands apart here. In Britain, the burden was placed on veterans to prove their case. But how do you claim what happened decades earlier when potentially vital records are missing or inaccessible?

In 2007, about 1,000 nuclear test veterans and families took the MoD to court seeking compensation. Pilots had been instructed to fly through mushroom clouds. Service personnel sailed and crawled through fallout. Others witnessed nuclear explosions, in some cases just two miles from ground zero. Surely our service personnel deserved better?

This is where the scandal turns ugly. To deal with the veterans’ litigation, the MoD instructed the Atomic Weapons Establishment (AWE) to collate relevant documentation into a searchable database called Merlin. More than 28,000 documents were eventually assembled, covering radiation, precautions, health monitoring and what was known about the possible biological effects of the tests. Yet the veterans’ lawyers had no practical access to this vast archive. Thanks to the extraordinary investigative journalism of Susie Boniface, historical documents began emerging referring to blood and urine testing.

When I saw the evidence, I raised it in November 2022 as chair of the defence committee. The MoD finally acknowledged that the AWE held copies of blood-test results and urine-radioactivity measurements for “a small number of individuals”. That took me straight back to my parliamentary answer four years earlier.

I challenged the then defence secretary, Ben Wallace . If this information existed within the MoD, why had ministers not been given the full picture? He agreed that withholding relevant medical information would be “deeply wrong” and undertook to investigate.

The dam was beginning to burst. Searches of Merlin for “blood” and “urine” subsequently identified 151 documents. Then another extraordinary twist. A software change meant the AWE could no longer provide a historical audit trail showing who had accessed Merlin.

In 2024 (after the general election), the government finally ordered a discovery exercise into what blood and urine testing had taken place. Its findings , published this July, are damning. Evidence indicates that medical examinations or blood testing were required for “the majority, if not all” of Britain’s nuclear-testing period, across all three armed services. Bizarrely, the review says it found no evidence of intentional concealment.

But after seven decades of incomplete answers and ministers kept in the dark, this cannot be where the story ends. Had veterans and their doctors known the full picture decades ago, cancers and other illnesses could have been diagnosed earlier. Lives could have been saved.

Merlin is now being transferred to the National Archives. But declassifying 28,000 documents into the public domain will take time and is not the same as giving veterans answers. Many are now in their 80s and 90s.

Given the numbers of veterans involved and the decades this has been allowed to drag on, this is arguably one of Britain’s biggest scandals – alongside infected blood, Windrush and the Post Office. It demands an apology to the nation from the prime minister, an independent tribunal to establish the truth, and a compensation scheme for veterans and widows similar to that provided in the US.

These men served their country. Their country failed them. Seventy years on, veterans should not still be fighting their own government for the truth.

Tobias Ellwood is a former defence minister and the author of Ten Steps to Prevent World War Three

editorials.title: The September reset is real. I’m about to become a better person, flaxseed by flaxseed
editorials.passage:
A re you a January resolutions or a September reset person? The latter has always felt more propitious to me, light of the exhaustion of Christmas and with the weather still on our side. Last week, when the Pavlovian response to buying new stationery (for my kids) kicked in, I found myself following a rote impulse to sort my life out by replacing the bag in the vacuum cleaner and committing to an unsustainable course of personal change. This is it! The beginning of a new way of life, driven by sharp pencils and the crispness of autumn.

I mean, it won’t last. But while most of us have read enough advisories cautioning against new year resolutions as durable, somehow September still promises the earth. I can’t shake it. As soon as the breeze picks up and the leaves start to turn, I feel my pilot light ignite – and the urge to sign up to unaffordable personal training sets in. It feels like an ancient response. I’m not writing this while leaning on a dry stone wall or managing my sheepdogs, but still; the sensory changes brought in by autumn surely activate latent energies in all of us. If you can avoid pumpkin spice and survive the costume search for Halloween, September triggers good feelings of renewal via the psychic memory of our serf forebears bringing in the harvest.

Or, in my case, attempting to do 10 minutes of squats and move last night’s dishes from the sink to the dishwasher before lunchtime. As ever when trying to implement new habits, the question is how you trick yourself into making them stick. It’s like that classic scene from Road Runner, when, running out beyond the edge of the cliff, Wile E Coyote keeps going until he looks down and drops like a stone. Will a magnetised whiteboard, stuck to the fridge, keep me running on thin air for a bit longer? What about a new trainer, texting me motivational messages – “let’s go soldier mode!” – at 7am every day? After all these years of failed resolutions, has the answer to fixing my life really resided in buying sandwich bags for the efficient storage of leftovers?

This is part of the problem, of course: that any commitment to change is used by most of us as a pretext to spend money. I assume that, in medieval times, the serf stockpiling for winter didn’t believe that the key to surviving til spring lay in a trip to the Container Store or buying a bar-grade blender. We can’t buy our way into new habits (although, I have to say, my new blender is amazing) unless it’s backed up with behavioural changes that come from – who knows?

Panic, probably. Which is why, in spite of all the scepticism, it still feels to me as if the September reset is real . As someone pointed out to me yesterday, it marks the entry point into the spookiest season, which means different things as we age. Influencers can run the clock on our finite number of summers, but as you get older it’s the onset of autumn that really turns up the burner on our sense of time passing. Foreshadowing death, the urge to get an arsing move on at this time of year is strong, and although it’s a line or argument that worries me – not least because it means I share psychological traits with eg notoriously crisis-surfing ex prime minister Boris Johnson – I’ve always considered panic a much underrated motivational force.

And so, this year, I’ve gone to the literature for help in utilising the September force and discovered there’s a whole movement around it. Contrary to new year, when we tank our chances of success before we’ve even started by creating goals that are too large to achieve, September offers a lower pressure context in which to implement small change. Small change is good! Small change is, they say, where it all happens. Ten-minute workouts. Going to bed an hour earlier. Being more open to popular life hacks such as, “keep a gratitude journal” (no).

If it feels like deckchairs on the Titanic, given the way the world is right now, we can control only what we can control. Will a collapse in the bond market crash all our futures, if the climate crisis doesn’t get us first? While I think about that, there’s a small chance that if I chip off the crust around the base of the kitchen tap, clear the drift of receipts from the bottom of my bag and put flaxseed into everything I eat, maybe all will be well.

Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnist

editorials.title: Trumpism is changing world order
editorials.passage:
The post-World War II era was dominated by idealism that gave birth to a dense architecture of multilateral institutions and Western-led governance frameworks.

That order has now reached a decisive historical inflection point. The foreign policy paradigm forged during the two administrations of United States President Donald Trump — marked by unilateralism, transactional nationalism, and a recalibration of historic alliances — represents a sharp break from prior international norms. Combining coercive leverage with strategic media manipulation, this shift has heralded a new foreign policy phenomenon: Trumpism.

By combining assertions of national sovereignty with an anti-establishment tone, Trumpism systematically challenges the core assumptions that had underpinned global governance for generations.

At its core, it represents a deliberate move away from grand, Western-dominated global leadership towards a decentralised, issue-specific, and deeply transactional international order.

Trumpism’s operational strategy has replaced traditional multilateral commitments with a hardheaded focus on economic statecraft and national interest. Foreign policy engagements have been explicitly tethered to domestic economic priorities: reindustrialisation, a revitalised defence industrial base, energy dominance, balanced trade, and leadership in the financial sector.

To achieve these aims, the Trump administration has eschewed expansive multinational agreements in favour of bilateral bargains, deploying aggressive tariffs, coercive trade measures, and sanctions as primary instruments of state power.

The administration’s reliance on expansive sanctions regimes and aggressive extraterritorial enforcement has ignited fierce global debates regarding international law, state sovereignty, and the legitimate limits of national jurisdiction.

Under the banner of “peace through strength”, Trumpism has integrated legal, economic, and security mechanisms to pressure allies and adversaries alike. Law enforcement operations and national security objectives have been routinely repurposed as direct tools of foreign policy.

This transactional posture has extended directly into collective defence and security architectures, most notably NATO. Trumpism has brought intense scrutiny to Western defence burden-sharing arrangements, highlighting severe imbalances where the US had borne a disproportionate share of costs and strategic risks.

The systemic consequences of Trumpism have reverberated across every layer of the global governance hierarchy.

In multilateral forums, the administration has displayed unprecedented ambivalence and unpredictability, frequently reneging on established international agreements and disengaging from multilateral institutions.

This volatile leadership style has exposed deep vulnerabilities within global governance, accelerating the fragmentation of the post-Cold War liberal international order.

A prominent casualty of this institutional disruption has been the United Nations, particularly the UN Security Council. Trump’s policies have magnified existing debates over the UNSC’s legitimacy, representation, and effectiveness.

Observers have noted that entrenched geopolitical rivalries, institutional inertia, and structural hierarchies rooted in the colonial era had already left the UNSC paralysed—trapped in a pre-contemplation stage of reform rather than delivering substantive structural changes. US institutional disengagement has further compounded this inertia, raising fundamental questions about the long-term durability and authority of international security bodies.

While proponents have argued that the Trump administration is seeking to drive necessary institutional reform through selective, high-level engagement—such as collaborating with like-minded allies and engaging the UN secretary-general on shared priorities—critics have viewed these moves as prioritising immediate national interests over global stability.

As the US is stepping back from global stewardship, the resulting power vacuum is catalysing a profound restructuring of international politics. Middle powers and regional blocs are increasingly stepping forward to bridge governance gaps.

These actors have begun constructing regional frameworks and issue-specific coalitions, casting them as vital supplements — or direct alternatives — to traditional Western-dominated institutions.

This global pivot has ignited a fierce debate among international relations scholars and policymakers regarding Trump’s legacy.

On the one hand, some argue that the disruptions he has caused are a catalyst for reform and systemic resilience. By forcing middle powers and non-Western nations to take greater ownership of regional security and economic coordination, Trumpism is fostering a more plural, inclusive, and realistic global order capable of addressing modern geopolitical realities.

Others are warning that US disengagement from multilateral commitments has shattered collective security arrangements and degraded institutional legitimacy. From this viewpoint, weakened Western leadership has paved the way for sustained strategic competition, regional instability, and dangerous governance voids across critical international forums.

The foreign policy of the Trump presidency cannot be dismissed as a temporary aberration or a simple shift in personal political style; it warrants the enduring label Trumpism because it has established a distinct, reproducible paradigm of international statecraft.

By deliberately weaponising unpredictable diplomacy, prioritising national prosperity over institutional continuity, and asserting absolute national sovereignty against global governance constraints, Trumpism fundamentally is redefining how a great power can exercise leverage in the modern era.

Trump’s foreign policy will leave an indelible imprint on the contemporary international system. By challenging the foundational premises of the liberal international order, it will permanently alter the balance of power, forcing the world into a new era characterised by decentralised authority, heightened regionalism, and a continuous search for new governance models.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

editorials.title: Flood risks to Nepal hydropower project were known – but banks ignored them
editorials.passage:
On August 26, Samar Bezbaruah was preparing for a regular day. He had left his home in Assam’s Nalbari district seven months earlier to work in Nepal’s 216-MW Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project. That morning, he walked into the project’s tunnel with a group of 20 others to begin the day’s work.

At around 9.15 am, from within the tunnel, the group saw a colossal mass of water slam into the powerhouse of the project, which was situated in the river valley below them, and in which some colleagues were working.

Bezbaruah and the others rushed out of the tunnel to get to a safer place. Now they saw the full extent of the destruction – roads below had all been engulfed by the crashing water, silt and debris.

“We then climbed a nearby hill,” Bezbaruah told Scroll . “We waited for two days there before we were rescued.”

Bezbaruah returned to his village on Monday evening. Many of his colleagues could not. “From Assam, we were a group of 13, and of these only eight have returned home,” he said. “We do not even know where the rest are. One of them was a relative from my village, we have not been able to contact him.”

He added, “The powerhouse also had people from Himachal, Punjab, Uttar Pradesh. So many of them are missing.”

In all, around 350 workers were rescued from the affected hydropower projects in the days after the flood, but rescue operations had to halt because a risk arose of another flood. Operations have now resumed; currently, more than 600 workers are still missing.

Among those rescued from Upper Trishuli-1 are 73 Indians , including Bezbaruah. According to the Indian Express , around 150 Indian and Nepali workers on the project are still missing. “Most of the workers here were Indians,” said Bezbaruah.

The project is the largest of the 13 hydropower projects damaged or destroyed by the flood. It is the second in a series of projects on the river, around 35 km downstream from the Tibet-Nepal border, where the flood first hit.

It is funded through loans by the Asian Development Bank , or ADB, and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, or AIIB, which put a combined $150 million in loans into the dam, making it one of the largest foreign direct investments in Nepal’s history.

Even as rescue operations continue, public reports of the project show that project authorities and the funding banks failed to adequately assess the risks it faced of climate-related disasters.

A 2018 environmental and social assessment report of the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank noted that there is “minimum GLOF threat in the project area”, referring to glacial lake outburst floods. Of the three identified glaciers in the region, it noted, “none are considered under the high risk GLOF category”.

Meanwhile, in December 2024, an independent panel of experts visited the site as a part of routine monitoring for the Asian Development Bank. In their report they wrote that “no climate resilience assessment was undertaken for the Project – this is a significant gap”. It then recommended that such an assessment be conducted.

However, a year later in May 2025, the panel for the ADB found that the assessment “has yet to be done”.

These lapses were noted by researchers Parineeta Dandekar and Himanshu Thakkar, who are associated with the South Asia Network on Dams, Rivers and People. In one post, they wrote that while the international banks’ own reports repeatedly highlighted climate risks, “they did not take any preventive steps, did not demand stringent checks and balances, nor were they prepared for a calamity they knew could occur”.

The banks funded the projects in the name of “climate and disaster resilience, something that sounds especially jarring today”, they wrote in another post.

Prabindra Shakya, founder of Kathmandu-based Community Empowerment and Social Justice Network, said that in the Trishuli river valley, “climate impact assessment should have been a major consideration, because this is not the first time we have seen floods here”. He added, “We had a glacial lake outburst last year too.”

The banks’ failures were particularly serious because their “policies outline that they need to look into these risks”, said Sunil Acharya, who is based in Kathmandu, and who is the Lead of Just Transition for the international non-profit advocacy group Recourse. “There is a clear lapse of their own accountability duties,” Acharya said. “These projects are simply being pushed through.”

Scroll emailed the project’s funding banks, and the project authorities, seeking responses to criticism that they had not adequately assessed the safety risks to the project. This story will be updated if they respond.

Hydropower accounts for almost all of Nepal’s installed electricity generation capacity of 4,120 MW. “Nepal’s dream of becoming a developed country is by exploiting hydropower,” Acharya said. “Over 98% of the country’s electricity comes from hydropower.”

He explained that all of the country’s fossil fuel is imported and that it saw these projects as a path out of dependence on imports. “This dream was then pushed by international finance institutions,” he said.

Several of these projects depend on international financing – as data collated by the International Accountability Project shows, between 2016 and 2026, the Asian Development Bank, the United States’ Development Finance Corporation, and the World Bank’s International Finance Corporation have approved loans, grants and “advisory services” for at least six projects related to hydropower. Ten more are in the “proposed” stage.

As Dandekar and Thakkar, noted , a “cumulative impact assessment” of the Trishuli basin, published by the International Finance Corporation in 2020, analysed potential environmental and social impacts of hydropower across the entire the basin, but did not discuss the threats of glacial lake outburst floods and flood disasters. While it looked at the fragmentation of aquatic habitat, reduced water availability and impacts on river-based livelihoods in the basin, which has more than 36 hydropower projects, “It did not even attempt to look upstream and assess Tibetan impacts,” they wrote. “It made no cumulative disaster plan for a basin littered with hydropower projects.”

In fact, a few months before December 2024, when the independent panel suggested a climate assessment, the basin saw clear indications of risks to the project. Specifically, on September 28, the Nepal government issued a warning about a risk of high rainfall – by noon that day, parts of the project had collapsed due to rising river water.

In its May assessment, where it found that the assessment it had recommended had not yet been done, the panel also noted that the September flood showed that “combinations of climatic and geological events can have severe consequences”. It recommended “expanding the scope of such climate resilience assessment to disaster risks”.

“The project should not have gone ahead without a climate assessment in the first place,” said Vaishnavi Vardarajan, Asia Pacific Program Coordinator at the International Accountability Project.

Once the project did go forward, she noted, the irony was that “the bank themselves asked this expert body to come together”. Despite this, “its recommendations have not become a part of the bank’s due diligence and have not changed the trajectory of the project.”

She added, “It is a clear sign that the banks are not following their own systems of accountability.”

The failure to carry out the recommended assessment of the Upper Trishuli-1 project was not the authorities’ only lapse. The panel had recommended that the project’s “early warning system” should be redesigned “as soon as possible”. But, by May 2025, not much had changed. “The slow implementation of a reliable early flood warning system… remains a major risk to those project communities in proximity to the river,” the panel’s report noted.

Bezbaruah told Scroll that the project was equipped with a siren that would go off if water suddenly rose near the tunnel, or even if there was any other emergency. “But we do not know what happened that day, it did not go off,” he said. “We had no time to think or to speak when the waters came in.

The panel also found that muck from the project was being disposed of directly in the river, a practice that is known to worsen the impacts of floods, since the debris causes additional damage. Muck seems to be “disposed where convenient to the contractor”, it noted. In many instances, the muck had been dumped along “gabions”, which refers to retaining walls – these “had actually collapsed during the monsoon and materials were washed away by the river”, the panel found.

The Upper Trishuli-1 project was not the only one that the December 2024 report raised concerns about. It also found that an early warning system installed 10 km upstream in the Chilime hydropower project “proved to be useless” for the flood that September. The Chilime project has been severely impacted by the flood last week and at least eight workers on it are missing.

Experts noted that the recent disaster is not an isolated event, and that Nepal has seen numerous instances in the past of hydropower projects suffering damage from climate-related events. Between 2015 and 2020, for instance, floods and landslides damaged 34 hydropower projects. A few years later, in just the month of June 2023, torrential rain in Eastern Nepal caused floods that damaged 30 hydropower projects. “Despite these challenges, Nepal still lacks a Basin-specific, climate-responsive framework to guide long-term hydropower and water resource planning,” researchers Sanju Adhikary and Mahendra Aryal wrote in a June 2026 paper.

While the resulting threat to safety is the most serious concern, experts have also noted that when financial institutions overlook climate risks of hydropower projects, the borrowing nation can be left with heavy debt burdens.

Acharya gave the example of the Melamchi Water Supply Project, funded by the Asian Development, OPEC fund for International Development, Nordic Development Fund and Japan Bank for International Cooperation. In 2021, the project’s infrastructure suffered damage because of a flood, just before it was supposed to begin functioning. “ADB had not done an assessment of the climate risks. Now, the project only works partially, and Nepal is continuing to pay the loan back,” said Acharya.

In light of these crises, Nepal needed to reevaluate its energy future, experts said. “Nepal should invest more in diversifying its energy means,” said Acharya. “It should invest in distributed solar and wind, and in making the power grid more climate resilient.” He added that this responsibility also fell on financial institutions, and that they needed to fund renewable energy projects other than hydropower.

Vardarajan echoed this argument, adding that banks needed to evaluate projects more rigorously. “Climate analysis has to appear urgently in international banks’ risk rating of a project,” said Vardarajan. “Multiple disasters have happened in the Himalayan region.” If banks did not conduct such assessments, “they are just bankrolling climate disasters”, she said.

Shakya suggested that smaller and medium-scale hydroprojects could be less risky. “In our work we have been piloting and supporting through financial and technical assistance for community-led micro hydroprojects less than 20KW,” he said. Such decentralised small and medium level projects, he argued, can be a more environmentally and socially viable option “rather than a cascade of large scale dams”.
