editorials.title: The Indus Waters Treaty: India will not back down
editorials.passage:
On August 31, a Court of Arbitration (CoA) constituted by the World Bank under the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) to consider Pakistan’s objections to certain aspects of India’s Kishanganga Hydel Electric Project (KHEP) and the Ratle Hydro Electric Project (RHEP) gave an award in Islamabad’s favour. India had not taken part in the CoA’s proceedings because, as a statement from the Ministry of External Affairs noted, “This so-called Court was constituted by the World Bank in patent breach of the terms of the Treaty and India categorically rejects its so-called award, just as it has firmly rejected all prior pronouncements by this illegally constituted body”.

The statement went on to add, “This so-called Court of Arbitration has no jurisdiction whatsoever to pronounce on India’s sovereign decisions. Its pronouncements, now or in the future, will have no effect on India’s actions in connection with the projects being undertaken by India”. The statement also categorically affirmed, “India’s decision to hold the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance remains in force”. It is good that India swiftly rejected the CoA’s award and confirmed that it would have no impact on India’s decision to hold the IWT in abeyance until Pakistan demonstrably abandons the path of terrorism.

This article will only slightly touch upon the technicalities of the issues. It will examine how the World Bank, which is assigned a role in the treaty, mishandled the situation. It will also look at the CoA’s mentality on the issue of terrorism. Finally, it will look at how Pakistan’s continuing policies on terrorism and approaches to the IWT will inevitably lead to India continuing to ignore it. The CoA’s award, along with Pakistan raising the IWT internationally in the guise of ‘weaponisation of water’, cannot but lead India to disregard it.
The World Bank’s Role
The IWT gives the waters of the Ravi, Sutlej and Beas entirely for India’s use. They are called the Eastern Rivers under the treaty. Pakistan has the rights to the waters of the Chenab, Jhelum and Indus. They are called the Western Rivers in the treaty. India is allowed to use a marginal portion of the Western Rivers’ waters too and is allowed to generate electric power on them in ‘run-of-the-river’ projects. Ever since the Treaty was signed in 1960, Pakistan has, in a ‘Pavlovian’ manner, impeded every hydroelectric project India has planned on the Western Rivers, including RHEP and KHEP.

The IWT includes an India-Pakistan Indus Waters Commission for its orderly implementation. Pakistani objections to the projects are first sought to be resolved by the Commission. If it fails, the issue/s are referred to the governments. If they cannot resolve them, the Dispute Resolution Mechanism (DRM) goes beyond the bilateral level. The World Bank, which played a great role in the making of the IWT, has a role in the implementation of the DRM. The Mechanism prescribes that technical issues go to a neutral expert and, for issues involving legal interpretations of the IWT, a CoA is to be formed. The manner of the appointments of both is prescribed in the IWT.

India’s view broadly is that it is only when a neutral expert states that the matter goes beyond technical issues that a CoA should be convened. Pakistan insists that both processes can take place simultaneously. A CoA in 2013 largely agreed with Pakistan. However, Indian objections continued and, in 2014-16, Pakistan urged the World Bank to appoint a CoA for the two projects. India argued that a neutral expert could look into what were purely technical issues. It told the Bank that there was simply no place for two adjudication processes to take place simultaneously. This was despite the 2013 decision.

The Bank, confronted with contradictory Indian and Pakistani requests, initially decided to act upon both. However, as the CoA notes, “On 12 December 2016, the President of the World Bank notified the Parties that the World Bank had decided ‘to pause the process of appointing the Chairman of the Court of Arbitration and the Neutral Expert’.” He explained, “I take this step in the interest of preserving the Treaty and in order to provide a window to further explore whether Pakistan and India can agree on a way forward for resolving the matter relating to the two hydroelectric power plants, in a manner that is satisfactory to both countries”.

The significant words in the World Bank’s decision to pause proceedings are “I take this step in order to preserve the Treaty…”. The rest are mere exhortations to both countries. These words show that the Bank was aware, despite a CoA’s 2013 ruling, that proceeding on both tracks simultaneously risked the treaty itself. That is the reason why it continued with the pause for over five years. On March 31, 2022, though, it informed both countries that it was lifting the pause.

The World Bank takes its cue from US administrations. Thus, its decisions on sensitive issues are driven from behind the scenes by the US, though it should resist US pressures. It clearly did not choose to do so in regard to the IWT. This is illustrated by the timing of the pause and its lifting. The pause was taken when Trump was US President-elect and continued throughout his first term. This was the period when India-US ties were becoming more consolidated.

When the pause was lifted, Biden had become President. The warmth in India-US ties cooled under him, though they remained correct. Besides, Biden’s liberal supporters were irked by some Indian approaches. It would not be wrong to assume that the Biden administration was also keen to appear neutral on the IWT between India and Pakistan. What it ignored, as did the World Bank in lifting the pause, was the fear which had led to it — that the pursuit of simultaneous processes despite Indian objections would jeopardise the treaty itself. That is precisely what is happening now.
The CoA and Terrorism
The CoA pursued a dichotomous approach on the impact of terrorism on the IWT. This is obvious from the difference between its press release on the award and its order that India could not hold the treaty in abeyance and that its doing so did not impact the CoA’s jurisdiction over the issues before it. The press release noted, “The Court then considered India’s allegations that Pakistan’s sponsorship of cross-border terrorism had impeded the utilisation of its rights under the Treaty. The Court noted that it took this allegation extremely seriously”.

However, how seriously it considered cross-border terrorism is illustrated by its characterisation of the heinous Pahalgam attack. The language it used shows its mentality. It stated, “On 23 April 2025, following an attack by armed individuals in India-administered Jammu and Kashmir, the Foreign Secretary of India issued a statement about a decision of the Cabinet Committee on Security (‘23 April Statement’), indicating, among other things, that ‘(t)he Indus Waters Treaty of 1960 will be held in abeyance with immediate effect, until Pakistan credibly and irrevocably abjures its support for cross-border terrorism’.”

What stands out is that the CoA decided to reduce the Pahalgam massacre to “an attack by armed individuals in India-administered Jammu and Kashmir”. Admittedly, a CoA has to exercise restraint in the use of its words, but does that have to go to the extent of an unwillingness to call a heinous terrorist attack just that? Instead, this CoA, while considering the act which led to India’s decision to hold the IWT in abeyance, merely reduced it to “an attack by armed individuals”. This is not judicial restraint but a shirking of responsibility to call out terrorism. Indeed, by using these words, the CoA revealed itself as a cold-hearted set of judges totally oblivious to the decades of restraint shown by India in the face of horrendous acts of terror from Pakistan.

Judges cannot be blind and deaf to the situation which leads to a country with an impeccable record of being a good global citizen holding a treaty in abeyance. Indeed, no treaty can ever be insulated from attendant circumstances. That is the lesson of history, and it is obvious the CoA had tunnel vision as it proceeded to technically interpret various sections of the IWT. Hence, its claim that it took Indian charges seriously about how cross-border terrorism had impeded the operation of the IWT is hollow when it reduced the Pahalgam terrorist attack merely to “an attack by armed individuals”.
What Now
There is no way India can resile from the position it has taken that the CoA was illegally constituted. This is backed by the detailed letter it had sent to the World Bank when it lifted the pause in 2022. The CoA, however, held that India’s objections were untenable. It was hardly wise for it to do so because it was aware that the Bank had been worried that if it proceeded on both tracks of dispute resolution, it would jeopardise the treaty, especially as India was not taking part in its proceedings. It also did not take into account that states have the right to act in their supreme national interest. That entitles them to disregard arrangements, agreements and even treaties.

Pakistan can keep complaining about the weaponisation of water and can keep issuing threats, including those of a nuclear nature. These statements are made for domestic consumption. It is not India’s run-of-the-river projects on the Western Rivers that have impaired Pakistan’s water security but its sheer mismanagement of this precious resource.
Conclusion
The only way India-Pakistan relations can be normalised, which would include a new water-sharing arrangement, as India has already asked for that from Pakistan, is if it gives up terrorism. Pakistani generals will not do that. Certainly, Field Marshal Asim Munir is not the kind of visionary who will realise that Pakistan’s progress can only really be achieved through the establishment of good ties with India.

(The writer is a former Indian diplomat who served as India’s Ambassador to Afghanistan and Myanmar, and as secretary, the Ministry of External Affairs. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: ‘Fitna al-Hindustan’: Pakistan’s new narrative to turn Baloch insurgency into an Indian conspiracy
editorials.passage:
On August 24, the Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) claimed another attack on Pakistani forces in Mastung, alleging that an IED ambush killed 13 soldiers. The timing is significant. Only days earlier, Pakistan had announced major counter-terror operations across Balochistan while repeatedly describing insurgents as “Fitna al-Hindustan”.




The expression is not merely another rhetorical flourish in the India-Pakistan vocabulary. Pakistan has blamed India for Baloch insurgency for years, but what is changing is the institutionalisation of that allegation. In May 2025, Pakistan’s Interior Ministry directed government entities to refer to insurgent organisations operating in Balochistan as “Fitna al-Hindustan”, framing them as part of an alleged Indian-sponsored campaign of violence.




Since then, Pakistan has increasingly embedded alleged Indian sponsorship into the language used to describe its internal security crisis. The term has turned a political accusation into an official lens for interpreting violence in Balochistan and has become part of the Pakistani military’s routine description of its counter-terror operations.




That matters because states do not rename security threats without purpose. Naming determines how a conflict is understood, where responsibility is located and, eventually, how it is sold to audiences abroad.




Pakistan’s recent counter-terror operations make the shift particularly visible. On August 21, the Inter-Services Public Relations said security forces had killed 49 militants across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan. Thirty-seven of those killed in Balochistan were described as belonging to “Fitna al-Hindustan”. Earlier operations in Mastung, Washuk and Surab that month were framed through the same vocabulary.




Balochistan’s insurgency predates the current deterioration in India-Pakistan relations, as do the political disputes that have sustained separatist mobilisation in the province. Since Pakistan’s early years, the conflict has moved through several phases, shaped by disputes over provincial autonomy, political representation and control of natural resources, as well as allegations of enforced disappearances, uneven development and coercive state policy. These issues have also shaped the relationship between Baloch nationalism and Pakistan’s highly centralised security establishment.




None of this absolves armed organisations that attack civilians or Pakistani security personnel. Terrorism does not become legitimate because its perpetrators claim political demands. But acknowledging the history of an insurgency is different from legitimising its violence. By collapsing that history into “Fitna al-Hindustan”, Pakistan achieves something politically useful: an internal crisis acquires an external author.



From an insurgency to an Indian conspiracy



Pakistan has accused India of involvement in Balochistan for years. The difference now is the institutionalisation of that accusation. There is an important distinction between a government alleging foreign sponsorship of a particular attack and directing the machinery of the state to incorporate that allegation into the very name by which an entire category of insurgents is identified. In the latter case, the accusation no longer requires repetition; rather, it is built into the vocabulary itself.




Every military statement using “Fitna al-Hindustan” consequently performs two functions. It reports a Pakistani counter-terrorism operation, but simultaneously tells its audience how that violence should be interpreted: not principally as a manifestation of Pakistan’s internal political and security problems, but as another front in the country’s confrontation with India.




That is strategically valuable for Pakistan. It moves the discussion away from why Balochistan remains unstable despite decades of military operations and enormous investments in infrastructure. It also allows the Pakistani state to place very different security challenges within a common framework of foreign interference.




The construction is particularly striking because Pakistan faces more than one insurgent threat. In Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the state increasingly uses “Fitna al-Khawarij” for the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan and associated militants. In Balochistan, “Fitna al-Hindustan” attaches India directly to the nomenclature of the enemy. The vocabulary is therefore doing political work.



The international audience matters



There is also a reason India should resist treating this simply as propaganda intended for Pakistani domestic consumption. Pakistan is increasingly taking this argument to international audiences — India, Pakistan claims, cannot accuse it of sponsoring terrorism while avoiding scrutiny over allegations that India supports violence inside Pakistan.




India has already recognised the significance of this construction. At the United Nations Security Council in June, India’s Permanent Representative, Ambassador Parvathaneni Harish, attacked Pakistan’s official use of “Fitna al-Hindustan”, describing it as state-sponsored misinformation wrapped in religious terminology.




The confrontation reveals the larger contest underway. India has spent years attempting to establish Pakistan-sponsored cross-border terrorism as a central fact of the bilateral relationship. After the Pahalgam terrorist attack, that diplomatic effort acquired renewed urgency. Pakistan has an obvious incentive to complicate this narrative by presenting itself not simply as a country accused of exporting terrorism, but as a victim of terrorism allegedly sponsored by India.




This is where “Fitna al-Hindustan” becomes more than semantics. If repeated consistently — in military communiqués, diplomatic statements, press conferences and multilateral forums — the terminology helps construct an equivalence: India says Pakistan sponsors terrorism; Pakistan says India sponsors terrorism. For an international audience that does not follow the history of every insurgency in South Asia, repetition itself can blur distinctions.



Balochistan cannot simply be erased from the story



This is precisely why India’s response requires more sophistication than merely calling Pakistan hypocritical. Balochistan has its own political history. The province is strategically extraordinary as it borders Iran and Afghanistan, possesses a long Arabian Sea coastline and hosts Gwadar, a centrepiece of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor. Yet it has remained one of Pakistan’s most politically unsettled regions.




The security implications extend well beyond India and Pakistan. Chinese personnel and projects have repeatedly become targets of militant violence, making Balochistan’s stability directly relevant to Beijing’s interests and to the future of CPEC. Instability also intersects with the Iran-Pakistan border and the wider militant ecosystem around Afghanistan. Reducing all of this to India may be useful messaging, but it does little to explain why the conflict persists.




Indeed, there is a danger for Pakistan itself in externalising every manifestation of Baloch insurgency. A state convinced that the primary explanation for an insurgency lies outside its borders has less incentive to confront the political conditions that allow the insurgency to reproduce itself internally. Counter-terrorism can kill militants. It cannot, by itself, settle a political question.



India should contest the vocabulary, not inherit it



There is an equally important lesson for New Delhi. India should not respond to Pakistan’s narrative by romanticising Baloch insurgency or appearing indifferent to attacks on Pakistani civilians. Doing so would strengthen precisely the argument Pakistan is trying to internationalise.




Instead, India has a stronger case when it separates three questions that Pakistan’s new terminology attempts to merge: first, the legitimacy of Baloch political demands; second, the illegitimacy of terrorism against civilians; and third, Pakistan’s allegation of Indian sponsorship. They are not the same question.




If Pakistan produces ‘evidence’ of Indian responsibility for a particular act, that evidence can be examined on its merits. But attaching India administratively to every terrorist organisation operating in Balochistan reverses that evidentiary process. The conclusion is placed inside the name before the evidence is debated.




That is why the terminology deserves attention. Pakistan is not merely accusing India anymore. It is attempting to reorganise the language through which its internal security crisis is understood. And in geopolitics, vocabulary is rarely innocent. A phrase repeated often enough in domestic institutions eventually enters diplomatic documents; diplomatic language enters international reporting; and what began as a state’s preferred description can gradually become one of the competing frames through which outsiders understand a conflict.




The contest over “Fitna al-Hindustan” is therefore not really about a phrase. It is about whether Pakistan succeeds in converting a deeply rooted internal insurgency into another chapter of the India-Pakistan conflict and, in the process, constructing a convenient equivalence between the terrorism India says it has endured from across the border and the terrorism Pakistan increasingly says originates from India.




(The author writes on women’s rights, politics and law. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views)

editorials.title: 2022 Khargone Ram Navami Violence: No Convictions, No Justice, Questions Remain
editorials.passage: Four years after communal violence erupted in Khargone during Ram Navami in April 2022, the criminal justice process has yet to produce a conviction.Sixty-five cases were registered after the violence. Around 20 cases are still being heard in local courts at different stages, and around 60 accused remain untraced, according to police sources. Now, in one of the cases that reached judgment, a sessions court has acquitted all 11 accused. Over a month after the acquittal on 27 July, the Madhya Pradesh government is reviewing the verdict and is expected to challenge it in the High Court.The acquittal, however, does not mean that the violence did not happen. The sessions court has accepted that the incident took place. What the prosecution failed to establish was that these 11 men were responsible for the offences with which they were charged.That distinction is important. It also raises a larger question about the aftermath of the Khargone violence: If the riot happened, why has the State struggled to establish individual criminal responsibility for it?Khargone Violence Accused Arrested: Here’s What We Know So FarIn the aftermath of the recent judgment, Additional Government Public Prosecutor Yuvraj Gujrathi said the Madhya Pradesh government was in the process of obtaining permission to challenge the acquittal, as well as pointed to the difficulty faced by the prosecution during the trial.Witnesses did not support the prosecution, he said, and some turned hostile. Fear, according to Gujrathi, was one of the reasons. People were reluctant to stand up and identify those accused of participating in the violence because they feared what might happen to them and their families afterwards. Who would protect them? What safeguards would be available if those they identified returned to their locality?Some witnesses, he said, live in Muslim-majority areas and were worried about the safety of their families. But identification itself became a contentious issue. There was no test identification parade in the case. Gujrathi had earlier described this as a police lacuna. The police, however, offer a different explanation.A police officer, who was involved in the investigation, said there was no point in holding an identification parade because the FIR itself recorded that the rioters had covered their faces while participating in the violence. “If their faces were covered, there was no question of identifying them,” he reasoned.The two explanations expose the difficulty at the heart of the case. The prosecution said witnesses were unable or unwilling to identify the accused.The police said the circumstances described in the FIR made a conventional identification parade impractical. But that leaves the larger question unanswered: If the faces of the rioters were covered and there was no identification parade, how were the identities of those subsequently accused established?The answer becomes particularly important because the court ultimately found the evidence insufficient to convict the 11 men. Eight prosecution witnesses did not identify the accused. The identification evidence presented by the prosecution also faced difficulties, while forensic evidence did not substantiate some of the allegations against the accused.BJP Wins Riot-Hit Khargone, Defeating Sitting Congress MLA By Big MarginThe case, therefore, demonstrates one of the most difficult challenges in investigating communal violence: moving from the undeniable fact of collective violence to establishing the individual role of each accused.The two are not the same. A riot can be real. The guilt of an individual accused of participating in it still has to be proved. And that requires an investigation capable of establishing identity through credible and independent evidence. The question of electronic evidence is equally important. The government prosecutor said, "The footage could not be played  in the court." He said that there might be some technical problem behind it.  Given the difficulty over eyewitness identification, the footage could potentially have helped establish the role of individual accused. The question, therefore, is what happened to the evidence in the four years between the violence and the trial. Was the original footage preserved and examined, and what efforts were made to make it usable in court?These questions matter because when eyewitnesses fail to identify the accused and electronic evidence cannot be effectively presented, the prosecution's ability to establish individual guilt becomes considerably weaker.Once the immediate violence ends, investigators have to reconstruct events, identify individual perpetrators, preserve evidence, and build cases that can withstand scrutiny years later in a courtroom. Khargone's record raises questions about whether that transition was successfully made. The problem is visible beyond the 11-men case. Police sources say around 60 accused remain untraced. But even here, there is an important qualification. Police say many of these are not necessarily known individuals deliberately evading arrest.An officer involved in investigations revealed,"Their names in the cases are often generic and are not accompanied by sufficient identifying details such as the father's name, locality or other particulars. That makes it difficult for investigators to establish who exactly the person is and where they can be found."It is another indication of the basic problem facing the investigation: Identifying an individual accused after a riot is considerably harder than naming a suspect in the immediate aftermath. The political context makes the issue even more significant.The Khargone violence occurred roughly a year before the 2023 Madhya Pradesh Assembly election. At the time, then Chief Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan promised a forceful response. He declared, “There is no place for rioters on the soil of Madhya Pradesh… They will not be spared. Strictest action will be taken against them."The message was unmistakable: those responsible for the violence would face the full force of the State. But criminal justice operates according to a different logic.'Wall, Barricades Dividing Communities': Khargone Lives With Scars of ViolenceStrict action must ultimately be based on evidence. An FIR is not proof of guilt. An arrest is not proof of guilt. Being named as an accused is not proof of guilt. The State has to establish what each individual did.That is why the absence of a conviction so far deserves attention, even though around 20 cases remain pending in courts. It would be premature to declare that the entire Khargone prosecution has failed.The pending cases may still result in convictions. But four years after the violence, the absence of a conviction raises legitimate questions about the effectiveness of the investigation and prosecution.The Association for Protection of Civil Rights (APCR), which provided legal assistance to people accused in the cases, believes the problem was more fundamental. Zaid Pathan, coordinator of APCR Indore, tells The Quint that both Hindus and Muslims were involved in the violence but alleges that criminal cases were disproportionately registered against Muslims. He says people who were not involved in the violence were also jailed.These are serious allegations and need to be tested against the complete police and court records. But the acquittal of the 11 men makes it relevant to examine how suspects were selected, what evidence connected them to specific offences, and whether investigators adequately distinguished between those who participated in the violence and those who were merely suspected. Pathan says APCR provided legal assistance to the accused and fought their case, ultimately helping them secure an acquittal.He also says that the National Security Act (NSA) was invoked against him in connection with his activities relating to peace efforts in Khargone. His account points to the atmosphere in which the post-riot investigation and legal proceedings unfolded.But the fear was not limited to activists or accused persons. According to Gujrathi, witnesses themselves were afraid. They feared retaliation and worried about the safety of their families if they identified those accused of participating in the violence. That presents the State with a difficult challenge.A witness cannot reasonably be expected to risk the safety of his family merely to provide an identification. In communal violence cases, witness protection can become as important as the evidence itself. But where eyewitness identification is compromised by fear, or impossible because the perpetrators concealed their faces, the burden on investigators to collect independent evidence becomes even greater. CCTV footage, photographs, forensic material, mobile-phone data, location records and other forms of corroboration can potentially help establish an accused person's role.If those avenues are not adequately explored, the prosecution may eventually be left with little more than statements that do not survive the trial. The acquittal of the 11 men should, therefore, be understood carefully. It does not establish that they were factually innocent.Nor does it erase the violence that Khargone witnessed in April 2022. It establishes that the prosecution failed to prove their guilt to the standard required by criminal law. That standard is not a technical obstacle to justice. It is the safeguard that separates suspicion from conviction.And it cuts both ways. If people who actually participated in the riots escape because investigators failed to collect sufficient evidence, the victims are denied justice. If people who did not participate are arrested and prosecuted because investigators failed to establish their identity or role properly, they too are denied justice. Both outcomes weaken public faith in the law. This is why the government's proposed appeal against the acquittal should be accompanied with a broader examination of the Khargone investigation. But an appeal can determine whether the trial court correctly assessed the evidence before it. It cannot retrospectively create evidence that investigators failed to collect. The High Court may eventually decide whether the acquittal of the 11 men was justified. But the more uncomfortable questions remain. Why was there no test identification parade? Was the police right that it would have served no purpose because the rioters' faces were covered? If so, what other identification methods were used? How much CCTV and video evidence was available, and how much of it could actually be examined? Why do around 60 accused remain untraced, and why were so many recorded without sufficient identifying particulars? And why, four years after the violence, has there been no conviction in any of the cases? Sajjan Kumar Is Dead. The Language Used to Protect Him Lives OnThe answers matter because the objective of a riot investigation should not be to produce a particular number of arrests. It should be to identify the people who committed specific crimes and build cases strong enough to prove those allegations in court.The political system can promise the “strictest action”. The police can register cases. The government can appeal an acquittal. But, ultimately, the courtroom asks a narrower question: "Who did what and where is the evidence?"The violence in Khargone was real. The demand for justice is real too. But justice requires both things to be true at the same time: that those responsible are punished, and that those who cannot be proved responsible are not. Four years later, Khargone is still waiting for the criminal justice system to complete that task.(Deshdeep Saxena is an independent journalist reporting on news and politics from Madhya Pradesh.)
